Audit the infrastructure code your task names, or your own change, against AWS security practice.

Policy skill. For how to write the infrastructure in the first place, use the `cdk-engineer` or the
`terraform-engineer` skill, which prefer built-in grants and modules over hand-written policy.

With no path named, look for CDK (`cdk/`, `lib/`), CloudFormation (`*.template.json`, `*.yaml`), Terraform (`*.tf`),
or AWS SDK code with `list_files`; a reviewer starts from the files the patch changes.

## Step 0: Load Project Specs

If the repository has a SECURITY.md (or INFRA.md), read it with `read_file` for its rules; else the built-in rules
below.

SECURITY.md is the canonical source for: Lambda auth rules, S3 public access, IAM wildcard policy, Cognito flows, CORS, EC2 IMDSv2, secrets storage, and CodeBuild policy. Cite SECURITY.md in findings (e.g., *"Function URL with AuthType NONE forbidden per SECURITY.md:8"*).

## Step 1: Detect IaC Stack

Read config files to determine: CDK (Python/TypeScript), CloudFormation, Terraform, Pulumi, or raw SDK.

## Step 2: Security Policy Checks

### AWS Service Naming (in comments/docstrings)
- [ ] First mention per file uses full official name ("Amazon Bedrock AgentCore", "Amazon DynamoDB", "AWS Lambda", "Amazon API Gateway")
- [ ] CDK-nag suppression reasons use full service names
- [ ] boto3 client identifiers are fine as-is in code. Add a comment mapping to the full service name

### OpenAPI Specs
- [ ] OpenAPI specs include a global `security` block requiring authentication on all endpoints
- [ ] `components.securitySchemes` defines the auth method (e.g., `sigv4` for IAM, `bearerAuth` for JWT)
- [ ] Response schemas include `maxItems` on array properties to prevent unbounded responses

### Security Documentation
- [ ] `SECURITY.md` exists with threat model, data classification, shared responsibility model
- [ ] Module docstrings for infra code document security decisions (auth, encryption, network)
- [ ] CDK-nag suppressions all have documented justifications
- [ ] For CDK projects, integrate `cdk-nag` (Apache 2.0) to validate security policies at synthesis time. Suppress findings only with documented justification.

### IAM (Least Privilege)
- [ ] No Action: `*` in any policy
- [ ] No Resource: `*` except where AWS requires it (CloudWatch PutMetricData, CloudWatch Logs)
- [ ] Document every Resource: `*` with a comment explaining why
- [ ] Global Bedrock inference profiles use an empty region field in the foundation-model ARN (`arn:aws:bedrock:::foundation-model/<model-id>`), not a literal wildcard. Grant the inference-profile ARN, the in-region model ARN, and the global model ARN as three separate statements, each scoped with `aws:RequestedRegion` and `bedrock:InferenceProfileArn` conditions. Never substitute a bare `Resource: "*"` for this
- [ ] IAM policy simulation (`simulate-principal-policy`, a person's check: it needs the account) also evaluates SCPs: pass `aws:RequestedRegion` in `--context-entries` or a region-guard SCP reports `explicitDeny` on every regional action
- [ ] No inline policies on Lambda roles (use managed + grant methods)
- [ ] Only AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole as managed policy (no AdministratorAccess, PowerUser)

### Secrets Management
- [ ] API keys, passwords, tokens in SSM Parameter Store (SecureString) or Secrets Manager
- [ ] Never in Lambda environment variables as plaintext
- [ ] Never in CDK code as string literals
- [ ] SSM parameters holding secrets use type `SecureString` with a CMK. Standard tier is encrypted; Advanced is only for values over 4 KB, over 10,000 parameters, or parameter policies, and it costs extra
- [ ] WithDecryption=True when reading secrets

### S3 Buckets
- [ ] block_public_access=BLOCK_ALL on every bucket
- [ ] enforce_ssl=True (deny non-HTTPS)
- [ ] encryption enabled (S3_MANAGED minimum, KMS preferred for prod)
- [ ] versioned=True for data buckets
- [ ] Lifecycle rules for cost management
- [ ] removal_policy gated on environment (DESTROY only for dev)
- [ ] auto_delete_objects only for dev

### DynamoDB
- [ ] Encryption enabled (AWS_MANAGED minimum, CUSTOMER_MANAGED for prod)
- [ ] Point-in-time recovery enabled
- [ ] Removal policy gated on environment
- [ ] PAY_PER_REQUEST billing for variable workloads

### Lambda
- [ ] Explicit timeout set (not default 3s or unbounded)
- [ ] Explicit memory_size set
- [ ] Log group with retention policy
- [ ] Log group has encryption comment (default AWS-managed; note CMK option for production)
- [ ] reserved_concurrent_executions for production (prevent runaway scaling)
- [ ] No environment variables containing secrets

### Key Management
- [ ] Key rotation policy documented in SECURITY.md or AWS_SECURITY_GUIDELINES.md
- [ ] Customer-managed KMS key examples provided for production (DynamoDB, CloudWatch Logs, Secrets Manager)
- [ ] Secrets Manager rotation schedule documented (30-90 day recommendation)
- [ ] `aws kms enable-key-rotation` command in hardening documentation

### API Gateway
- [ ] API key required on endpoints
- [ ] Usage plan with throttling (rate_limit + burst_limit)
- [ ] Quota configured (daily/monthly limits)
- [ ] CORS restricted to specific origins in production (not `*`)
- [ ] Access logging enabled
- [ ] WAF attached for production

### Networking
- [ ] VPC endpoints for S3/DynamoDB if Lambda runs in VPC
- [ ] Security groups follow least-privilege (no 0.0.0.0/0 ingress)
- [ ] Private subnets for compute, public only for load balancers

### Removal Policies
- [ ] Every DESTROY policy gated on environment check
- [ ] Pattern: `DESTROY if env == "dev" else RETAIN`
- [ ] No DESTROY in production (hard check)

## Step 3: Report

A reviewer writes each FAIL and WARN as a finding (`write_findings`); a builder puts the summary in its finish.

```
## AWS Security Policy Audit

### Summary: X FAIL / Y WARN / Z PASS

| # | Category | Check | Status | File:Line | Details |
```

## Step 4: Fix (the builder, within its change)

1. Fix all FAIL items in the code your change touches
2. Add environment gates on WARN items
3. Verify the fixes compile and synthesize (`cdk synth`, `terraform validate`, or the language's compile check)

A FAIL in code your task does not touch goes in your finish, not in your patch.

For design rationale behind each rule, see `references/design-decisions.md`.
For application-layer security (auth, input validation, dependencies), see the `security-audit` skill.
For CDK deployment validation, see the `cdk-doctor` skill.

# AWS Security: Design Decisions

Why each rule exists, told through the incidents that motivated them.

## No Lambda Function URLs with AuthType NONE

**Rule**: Never create Lambda Function URLs with `AuthType: NONE`.

**Battle story**: A developer created a Lambda Function URL for a health check endpoint, setting AuthType to NONE for simplicity. A security scanner flagged it as world-accessible. Before the team could remediate, the function was discovered via DNS enumeration and hit with 2M requests in one hour, costing $400 in Lambda invocations. The health check also leaked internal service names in its response.

**How to apply**: Use API Gateway with JWT authorizer or IAM auth. For internal health checks, use ALB health check targets, not public Lambda URLs.

## No IAM Principal "*"

**Rule**: Never add Lambda resource-based policies with `Principal: "*"`.

**Battle story**: A CDK construct added a resource-based policy with `Principal: "*"` to allow cross-account invocation. The developer intended to restrict via conditions but forgot the `Condition` block. Any AWS account could invoke the Lambda, which had read access to a DynamoDB table with customer data. The issue persisted for 3 weeks before a security review caught it.

**How to apply**: Use specific service principals (`lambda.amazonaws.com`, `apigateway.amazonaws.com`) with `SourceArn` conditions. For cross-account, use specific account IDs.

## No S3 Public Access

**Rule**: All S3 buckets must have `block_public_access=BLOCK_ALL`.

**Battle story**: An S3 bucket hosting static assets was configured with public-read ACL. A developer accidentally uploaded a `.env` file to the bucket during a deployment script error. The file contained database credentials. The bucket was indexed by GrayhatWarfare (S3 scanner) within hours.

**How to apply**: Set `block_public_access=BLOCK_ALL` on every bucket. For public content, use CloudFront with OAC (Origin Access Control), not direct S3 public access.

## No CORS allow_origins=["*"]

**Rule**: Always list specific allowed origins.

**Battle story**: Same pattern as the application-level CORS incident, but in API Gateway configuration. A CDK stack set `allow_origins=["*"]` for development and it was promoted to production unchanged. The API accepted authenticated requests from any origin, enabling a credential-stealing attack via a malicious site.

**How to apply**: Use environment-gated CORS origins: `["http://localhost:3000"]` for dev, `["https://app.example.com"]` for production. Never use wildcards.

## Resource-Based Policies Persist After URL Deletion

**Rule**: When removing a Lambda Function URL, also remove leftover resource-based policies.

**Battle story**: A team deleted a Lambda Function URL to address a security scanner's finding. The Function URL was gone, but the resource-based policy statement (`FunctionURLAllowPublicAccess`) persisted. The Lambda was still invocable by anyone with the invoke API, just not via the vanity URL. The finding reappeared because the underlying permission was unchanged.

**How to apply**: After deleting a Function URL, run `aws lambda get-policy --function-name <name>` and remove any statement with `Condition.StringEquals.lambda:FunctionUrlAuthType: NONE`.

## Environment-Gated Removal Policies

**Rule**: Every DESTROY removal policy must be gated on environment.

**Battle story**: A CDK stack used `RemovalPolicy.DESTROY` on a DynamoDB table for easy cleanup during development. The same stack was deployed to production without changing the removal policy. During a stack update that renamed the table's logical ID, CloudFormation deleted the production table with 2 years of data. Recovery required restoring from a point-in-time backup, causing 4 hours of downtime.

**How to apply**: Pattern: `RemovalPolicy.DESTROY if env == "dev" else RemovalPolicy.RETAIN`. Add `point_in_time_recovery=True` on all DynamoDB tables.

## Document Every Resource: "*"

**Rule**: Every `Resource: "*"` must have a comment explaining why.

**Battle story**: An IAM policy for a monitoring Lambda used `Resource: "*"` on `cloudwatch:PutMetricData`. This is actually correct (CloudWatch PutMetricData does not support resource-level permissions). However, during a security audit, the reviewer couldn't tell if this was intentional or lazy, and spent 2 hours investigating. Adding a comment (`# CloudWatch PutMetricData does not support resource-level permissions per AWS docs`) would have saved that time.

**How to apply**: For every `Resource: "*"`, add an inline comment citing the AWS documentation reason. Common exceptions: CloudWatch PutMetricData, CloudWatch Logs (CreateLogGroup), STS AssumeRole (when using global endpoint).

## Secrets Manager Over Environment Variables

**Rule**: Store secrets in Secrets Manager or SSM Parameter Store, not Lambda environment variables.

**Battle story**: A Lambda function stored an API key in an environment variable. The key was visible in the Lambda console to anyone with `lambda:GetFunctionConfiguration` permission, which was granted to the entire dev team via a broad IAM policy. A developer's laptop was compromised, giving the attacker read access to all Lambda configs and every secret stored as an environment variable.

**How to apply**: Store secrets in Secrets Manager with `aws_secretsmanager.Secret`. Grant the Lambda execution role `secretsmanager:GetSecretValue` scoped to the specific secret ARN. Read at runtime with caching.

## Global Inference Profiles: Three Scoped Statements, Not a Bare Wildcard

**Rule**: Grant Bedrock global cross-Region inference with three conditioned IAM statements, not `Resource: "*"`.

**Battle story**: A reviewer found `Resource: "*"` on `bedrock:InvokeModel` justified in a comment as "required for global inference profiles." AWS's own global cross-Region inference policy uses the opposite pattern: the global foundation-model ARN has an empty region field (`arn:aws:bedrock:::foundation-model/<model-id>`), and access is scoped with `aws:RequestedRegion` and `bedrock:InferenceProfileArn` conditions across three statements (inference-profile ARN, in-region model ARN, global model ARN). A flat `*` grants every model in every region, which the documented pattern never requires.

**How to apply**: Copy the three-statement policy from the AWS Bedrock global cross-Region inference guide. Never collapse it to a wildcard resource for convenience.

# Sources

Non-obvious claims verified against these sources, with the date checked.

| Claim | Source | Checked |
|---|---|---|
| Global Bedrock inference profiles use an empty-region foundation-model ARN (`arn:aws:bedrock:::foundation-model/<id>`) scoped via `aws:RequestedRegion` + `bedrock:InferenceProfileArn`, not a wildcard resource | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/global-cross-region-inference.html | 2026-10-28 |
| Geographic cross-Region inference profiles require three resource grants (profile, source-Region model, destination-Region models) | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/geographic-cross-region-inference.html | 2026-10-28 |
| cdk-nag is licensed Apache-2.0, current major version 3.x | https://github.com/cdklabs/cdk-nag (LICENSE, package.json) | 2026-10-28 |

---
name: aws-serverless
description: "Designs and reviews serverless apps on AWS Lambda, API Gateway, EventBridge, Step Functions, SQS and DynamoDB: limits, event sources, orchestration, SAM or CDK, observability, cold starts, cost, anti-patterns. Read it when writing or reviewing serverless code or IaC."

license: MIT
adapted: "Discovery uses list_files and read_file. The deployment step became IaC the agents write and validate offline (sam validate, cdk synth, sam local without Docker where possible); sam deploy, cdk deploy and cdk diff are a person's, since the run never deploys and has no account. Account commands in the references are marked as a person's. Slash references name library skills; deploy-on-aws (not vendored) is dropped; description and emphasis reworded for Claude 5.5 skill discovery"
---

Build or review the serverless application your task names.

## Step 1: Detect Serverless Stack

Look for existing serverless infrastructure with `list_files` and `read_file`:

- SAM projects: `template.yaml`, `template.yml`, `samconfig.toml`
- CDK projects: `cdk.json`, `bin/`, `lib/*stack*`
- Lambda functions: the handler files the templates or stacks name

Determine: SAM vs CDK, runtime (Python/TypeScript/Java), event sources, existing patterns.

## Step 2: Lambda Function Design

### Runtime Selection

| Language | When to Use | Powertools |
|---|---|---|
| TypeScript (default) | APIs, web backends, most use cases | Yes |
| Python | Data processing, ML inference, scripting | Yes |
| Java | Enterprise, high-throughput, Spring Boot | Yes |
| Rust | Ultra-low latency, cost optimization | Community |

### Function Structure (TypeScript)

```typescript
import { Logger } from '@aws-lambda-powertools/logger';
import { Tracer } from '@aws-lambda-powertools/tracer';
import { Metrics } from '@aws-lambda-powertools/metrics';

const logger = new Logger();
const tracer = new Tracer();
const metrics = new Metrics();

export const handler = async (event: APIGatewayProxyEventV2): Promise<APIGatewayProxyResultV2> => {
  const segment = tracer.getSegment();
  try {
    logger.info('Processing request', { path: event.rawPath });
    metrics.addMetric('RequestCount', 'Count', 1);

    // Business logic here

    return { statusCode: 200, body: JSON.stringify({ success: true }) };
  } catch (error) {
    logger.error('Request failed', { error });
    metrics.addMetric('ErrorCount', 'Count', 1);
    return { statusCode: 500, body: JSON.stringify({ error: 'Internal error' }) };
  }
};
```

### Function Configuration Checklist

- [ ] Explicit `timeout` set (not default 3s; max 900s)
- [ ] Explicit `memorySize` set (1 vCPU = 1769MB)
- [ ] Log group with retention policy (not infinite)
- [ ] X-Ray tracing enabled
- [ ] Dead letter queue for async invocations
- [ ] Reserved concurrency for production (prevent runaway scaling)
- [ ] Environment variables for config (never secrets)
- [ ] Secrets in SSM Parameter Store or Secrets Manager

### Lambda Limits Quick Reference

| Resource | Limit |
|---|---|
| Timeout | 900s (15 min) |
| Memory | 128MB – 10,240MB |
| Sync payload | 6MB request + 6MB response |
| Async payload | 1MB |
| Streamed response | 200MB |
| Package (uncompressed) | 250MB |
| Container image | 10GB |
| Layers | 5 per function |
| `/tmp` storage | 512MB – 10,240MB |
| Concurrent executions (default) | 1,000 |

## Step 3: Event Source Patterns

### API Gateway (REST/HTTP APIs)

| Feature | HTTP API (default) | REST API |
|---|---|---|
| Cost | $1.00/M requests | $3.50/M requests |
| Latency | Lower | Higher |
| Auth | JWT, IAM, Lambda | JWT, IAM, Lambda, Cognito, API keys |
| WebSocket | No | No (use WebSocket API) |
| Usage plans | No | Yes |

Default to HTTP API unless the task needs REST API features.

### Event Source Mapping (ESM) Patterns

| Source | Batch Size | Parallelization | Error Handling |
|---|---|---|---|
| DynamoDB Streams | 1-10,000 (default 100) | Up to 10 per shard | Bisect on error, max retries, DLQ |
| SQS | 1-10,000 (default 10) | Up to 1,000 | Visibility timeout, DLQ, partial batch |
| Kinesis | 1-10,000 (default 100) | Up to 10 per shard | Bisect on error, max retries |
| Kafka (MSK/self-managed) | 1-10,000 (default 100) | 1 per partition | DLQ |

### EventBridge Patterns

```typescript
// CDK: EventBridge rule → Lambda
const rule = new events.Rule(this, 'OrderRule', {
  eventPattern: {
    source: ['com.myapp.orders'],
    detailType: ['OrderCreated'],
  },
});
rule.addTarget(new targets.LambdaFunction(orderHandler, {
  retryAttempts: 2,
  deadLetterQueue: dlq,
}));
```

### S3 Event Notifications

```typescript
bucket.addEventNotification(
  s3.EventType.OBJECT_CREATED,
  new s3n.LambdaDestination(processUpload),
  { prefix: 'uploads/', suffix: '.csv' }
);
```

## Step 4: Step Functions & Orchestration

### When to Use What

| Pattern | Use Case | Service |
|---|---|---|
| Simple sequence | A → B → C | Step Functions (Express) |
| Long-running workflow | Human approval, wait states | Step Functions (Standard) |
| Fan-out/fan-in | Process items in parallel | Step Functions Distributed Map |
| Event choreography | Loose coupling, multiple consumers | EventBridge |
| Durable functions | Checkpoint/resume within Lambda | Lambda Durable Functions |
| Saga pattern | Distributed transactions with compensation | Step Functions or Lambda Durable Functions |

Lambda Durable Functions (GA December 2025) checkpoint and resume Node.js/Python handlers
natively via `context.step()` and `context.wait()`, pausing up to one year without compute
charges. Available in US East (Ohio), Python 3.13/3.14 and Node.js 22/24 only; use Step
Functions outside that region/runtime set.

### Step Functions Best Practices

- Use JSONata for data transformation (preferred over JSONPath)
- Add `Retry` on every Task state: `Lambda.ServiceException`, `Lambda.AWSLambdaException`
- Add `Catch` for business errors with fallback states
- Use SDK integrations to call AWS services directly (skip Lambda for simple operations)
- Use Distributed Map for processing large datasets (S3 items, DynamoDB scans)
- Express workflows for high-volume, short-duration (<5 min) workflows
- Standard workflows for long-running, auditable workflows

## Step 5: Infrastructure as Code (written here, deployed by a person)

The run never deploys and has no AWS account: write the template or stack, validate it offline, and leave the
deploy to a person.

### SAM

```bash
# Validate the template (offline lint)
sam validate --lint

# Build (a build that needs a container image needs Docker, which the sandbox does not have)
sam build

# A person deploys
sam deploy --guided  # First time
sam deploy           # Subsequent
```

### CDK

```bash
# Synth (offline; the `cdk-engineer` skill has the gate)
cdk synth

# A person diffs and deploys (both need the account)
cdk diff
cdk deploy --all --require-approval broadening
```

### CDK Serverless Constructs

```typescript
// Lambda with Powertools
const handler = new NodejsFunction(this, 'Handler', {
  entry: 'src/handler.ts',
  runtime: Runtime.NODEJS_20_X,
  timeout: Duration.seconds(30),
  memorySize: 512,
  tracing: Tracing.ACTIVE,
  logGroup: new LogGroup(this, 'HandlerLogs', { retention: RetentionDays.TWO_WEEKS }),
  environment: {
    POWERTOOLS_SERVICE_NAME: 'my-service',
    LOG_LEVEL: 'INFO',
  },
  bundling: {
    minify: true,
    sourceMap: true,
  },
});

// API Gateway HTTP API
const api = new HttpApi(this, 'Api', {
  corsPreflight: {
    allowOrigins: ['https://myapp.com'],
    allowMethods: [CorsHttpMethod.GET, CorsHttpMethod.POST],
  },
});
api.addRoutes({
  path: '/orders',
  methods: [HttpMethod.GET, HttpMethod.POST],
  integration: new HttpLambdaIntegration('OrdersIntegration', handler),
});
```

## Step 6: Observability

### Structured Logging (Powertools)

```typescript
logger.info('Order processed', {
  orderId: order.id,
  customerId: order.customerId,
  amount: order.total,
  duration: Date.now() - startTime,
});
```

### Key Metrics to Monitor

| Metric | Alarm Threshold | Action |
|---|---|---|
| Errors | > 1% of invocations | Page on-call |
| Duration | > 80% of timeout | Optimize or increase timeout |
| Throttles | > 0 | Increase reserved concurrency |
| ConcurrentExecutions | > 80% of limit | Request quota increase |
| IteratorAge (streams) | > 60s | Increase parallelization |
| DeadLetterErrors | > 0 | Investigate DLQ messages |

### X-Ray Tracing

Enable on Lambda + API Gateway + DynamoDB for end-to-end request tracing.

## Step 7: Performance Optimization

### Cold Start Reduction

| Technique | Impact | Effort |
|---|---|---|
| Smaller package size | High | Low |
| Provisioned concurrency | Eliminates cold starts | $$$ |
| SnapStart (Java, Python 3.12+, .NET 8+) | Up to 90% reduction | Low |
| ARM64 (Graviton) | 20% cheaper, similar perf | Low |
| Lazy initialization | Medium | Low |
| Tree-shaking (esbuild) | Medium | Low |

### Cost Optimization

- Use ARM64 (Graviton2), 20% cheaper, same or better performance
- Right-size memory with AWS Lambda Power Tuning
- Use Savings Plans for predictable workloads
- Prefer EventBridge over polling (SQS long-poll costs add up)
- Use S3 Express One Zone for high-frequency access patterns

## Anti-Patterns to Detect

| # | Anti-Pattern | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Lambda calling Lambda synchronously | Use Step Functions or SQS |
| 2 | No DLQ on async invocations | Add SQS DLQ |
| 3 | Secrets in environment variables | Use SSM/Secrets Manager |
| 4 | No timeout set | Set explicit timeout |
| 5 | Monolith Lambda (>250MB) | Split into focused functions |
| 6 | Polling DynamoDB for changes | Use DynamoDB Streams |
| 7 | No idempotency on writes | Use Powertools Idempotency |
| 8 | REST API when HTTP API suffices | Switch to HTTP API (cheaper) |
| 9 | Default 3s timeout | Set based on actual execution time + buffer |
| 10 | No retry/catch in Step Functions | Add Retry + Catch on every Task |

## Report

A reviewer writes each row as a finding (`write_findings`); a builder puts the summary in its finish.

```
## Serverless Review: [target]

### Stack: [SAM/CDK] + [Runtime] + [Event Sources]
### Summary: X MUST / Y SHOULD / Z NIT

| # | Category | Check | Status | File:Line | Details |
|---|----------|-------|--------|-----------|---------|
```

## Self-Check

- [ ] Every Lambda has explicit timeout and memory
- [ ] Every async invocation has a DLQ
- [ ] No secrets in environment variables
- [ ] Event source mappings have error handling (bisect, DLQ, max retries)
- [ ] Step Functions have Retry + Catch on Task states
- [ ] IAM policies are least-privilege (no wildcards)
- [ ] Structured logging with correlation IDs
- [ ] X-Ray tracing enabled

For CDK debugging, see the `cdk-doctor` skill.
For security hardening, see the `aws-security` skill.
For Lambda event source patterns, see `references/event-sources.md`.
For Step Functions patterns, see `references/step-functions.md`.
For optimization techniques, see `references/optimization.md`.
For verified sources on claims in this skill, see `references/sources.md`.

Gate before reporting done: `cdk synth` or `sam validate`, then the test command, reading each exit code (a person
reads `cdk diff` before they deploy). Then apply the `verification-before-completion` skill.

# AWS Serverless: Event Source Patterns

## Event Source Mapping (ESM) Configuration

### DynamoDB Streams

```yaml
# SAM template
Events:
  DynamoDBStream:
    Type: DynamoDB
    Properties:
      Stream: !GetAtt Table.StreamArn
      StartingPosition: TRIM_HORIZON
      BatchSize: 100
      MaximumBatchingWindowInSeconds: 5
      ParallelizationFactor: 10
      MaximumRetryAttempts: 3
      BisectBatchOnFunctionError: true
      DestinationConfig:
        OnFailure:
          Destination: !GetAtt DLQ.Arn
      FilterCriteria:
        Filters:
          - Pattern: '{"eventName": ["INSERT", "MODIFY"]}'
```

**Key settings:**
- `ParallelizationFactor`: 1–10 concurrent Lambda per shard (default 1)
- `BisectBatchOnFunctionError`: splits failed batch in half to isolate poison pill
- `FilterCriteria`: process only matching events (saves Lambda invocations)
- `StartingPosition`: TRIM_HORIZON (all) or LATEST (new only)

**IAM permissions needed:**
```json
{
  "Effect": "Allow",
  "Action": [
    "dynamodb:DescribeStream",
    "dynamodb:GetRecords",
    "dynamodb:GetShardIterator",
    "dynamodb:ListStreams"
  ],
  "Resource": "arn:aws:dynamodb:*:*:table/MyTable/stream/*"
}
```

### SQS

```yaml
Events:
  SQSEvent:
    Type: SQS
    Properties:
      Queue: !GetAtt Queue.Arn
      BatchSize: 10
      MaximumBatchingWindowInSeconds: 5
      FunctionResponseTypes:
        - ReportBatchItemFailures
```

**Key settings:**
- `FunctionResponseTypes: ReportBatchItemFailures`: return partial failures instead of retrying entire batch
- Visibility timeout should be 6x Lambda timeout
- Use DLQ on the SQS queue (not Lambda) with `maxReceiveCount: 3`

**Partial batch failure response:**
```typescript
export const handler = async (event: SQSEvent): Promise<SQSBatchResponse> => {
  const failures: SQSBatchItemFailure[] = [];
  for (const record of event.Records) {
    try {
      await processRecord(record);
    } catch (error) {
      failures.push({ itemIdentifier: record.messageId });
    }
  }
  return { batchItemFailures: failures };
};
```

### Kinesis Data Streams

```yaml
Events:
  KinesisStream:
    Type: Kinesis
    Properties:
      Stream: !GetAtt Stream.Arn
      StartingPosition: TRIM_HORIZON
      BatchSize: 100
      MaximumBatchingWindowInSeconds: 5
      ParallelizationFactor: 10
      MaximumRetryAttempts: 3
      BisectBatchOnFunctionError: true
      DestinationConfig:
        OnFailure:
          Destination: !GetAtt DLQ.Arn
```

**Key settings:**
- Same retry/bisect pattern as DynamoDB Streams
- Monitor `IteratorAge` metric, if increasing, consumer is falling behind
- Enhanced fan-out for dedicated throughput per consumer

### S3 Event Notifications

```typescript
// CDK
bucket.addEventNotification(
  s3.EventType.OBJECT_CREATED,
  new s3n.LambdaDestination(handler),
  { prefix: 'uploads/', suffix: '.csv' }
);
```

**Gotchas:**
- S3 notifications are at-least-once delivery, make handler idempotent
- Only one notification config per prefix/suffix combo per bucket
- For fan-out, use S3 → EventBridge → multiple targets

### Kafka (MSK / Self-Managed)

```yaml
Events:
  KafkaEvent:
    Type: MSK
    Properties:
      Stream: !Ref MSKCluster
      Topics:
        - my-topic
      StartingPosition: TRIM_HORIZON
      BatchSize: 100
```

**Key settings:**
- One Lambda invocation per partition
- Use VPC config for MSK (Lambda needs network access)
- Self-managed Kafka needs `SourceAccessConfigurations` for auth

## Event Filtering

Event filtering reduces Lambda invocations by filtering at the ESM level:

```yaml
FilterCriteria:
  Filters:
    # DynamoDB: only INSERT events for orders > $100
    - Pattern: '{"eventName": ["INSERT"], "dynamodb": {"NewImage": {"amount": {"N": [{"numeric": [">", 100]}]}}}}'

    # SQS: only messages with specific attribute
    - Pattern: '{"body": {"type": ["order.created"]}}'

    # Kinesis: filter on decoded data
    - Pattern: '{"data": {"status": ["ACTIVE"]}}'
```

**Rules:**
- Up to 5 filters per ESM (OR logic between filters)
- Filters use EventBridge pattern syntax
- Filtered-out events are discarded (not sent to DLQ)
- Saves cost by avoiding Lambda invocations for irrelevant events

## Error Handling Decision Tree

| Scenario | Strategy |
|---|---|
| Transient error (throttle, timeout) | Retry with backoff (ESM handles this) |
| Poison pill (bad data) | BisectBatchOnFunctionError isolates it |
| Persistent failure | Send to DLQ after max retries |
| Partial batch failure (SQS) | ReportBatchItemFailures |
| Order matters (streams) | MaxRetryAttempts + DLQ (don't skip) |
| Order doesn't matter (SQS) | Partial batch + DLQ |

# AWS Serverless: Optimization Patterns

## Cold Start Reduction

### What Causes Cold Starts

1. New execution environment provisioned (no warm container available)
2. Code downloaded and extracted
3. Runtime initialized
4. Handler module loaded (imports, global scope)

### Reduction Techniques

| Technique | Cold Start Impact | Cost Impact | Effort |
|---|---|---|---|
| ARM64 (Graviton2) | ~10% faster init | 20% cheaper | Minimal |
| Smaller package | Proportional to size reduction | None | Low |
| Tree-shaking (esbuild) | 30-60% smaller bundle | None | Low |
| Lazy imports | Defer unused modules | None | Low |
| Provisioned concurrency | Eliminates cold starts | $$$  | Low |
| SnapStart (Java, Python 3.12+, .NET 8+) | Up to ~90% reduction | None | Low |
| Keep-warm pings | Reduces frequency | Minimal | Low |

### Package Size Optimization

```typescript
// CDK: esbuild bundling with tree-shaking
new NodejsFunction(this, 'Handler', {
  entry: 'src/handler.ts',
  bundling: {
    minify: true,
    sourceMap: true,
    treeshaking: true,
    externalModules: ['@aws-sdk/*'],  // Use Lambda-provided SDK
  },
});
```

**Rules:**
- Exclude `@aws-sdk/*` from bundle (Lambda runtime includes it)
- Use `minify: true` for production
- Enable `sourceMap: true` for debugging (minimal size impact)
- Avoid importing entire libraries (`import { DynamoDB } from '@aws-sdk/client-dynamodb'` not `import AWS from 'aws-sdk'`)

### Lazy Initialization

```typescript
// BAD: loaded on every cold start even if not used
import { S3Client } from '@aws-sdk/client-s3';
const s3 = new S3Client({});

// GOOD: initialized only when needed
let s3: S3Client | undefined;
function getS3Client(): S3Client {
  if (!s3) s3 = new S3Client({});
  return s3;
}
```

## Memory Tuning

Lambda allocates CPU proportional to memory:
- 128MB = ~0.07 vCPU
- 1769MB = 1 vCPU
- 3538MB = 2 vCPU
- 10240MB = 6 vCPU

### Right-Sizing with Power Tuning

Use [AWS Lambda Power Tuning](https://github.com/alexcasalboni/aws-lambda-power-tuning) (a person runs it: it
deploys a state machine and invokes the function in the account):

```bash
# Deploy the state machine
sam deploy --template-file powertuning.yaml

# Run tuning
aws stepfunctions start-execution \
  --state-machine-arn arn:aws:states:...:powerTuningStateMachine \
  --input '{
    "lambdaARN": "arn:aws:lambda:...:MyFunction",
    "powerValues": [128, 256, 512, 1024, 1769, 3008],
    "num": 50,
    "payload": "{\"test\": true}"
  }'
```

**Rules:**
- More memory = more CPU = faster execution = potentially cheaper
- Sweet spot is usually where cost curve flattens
- CPU-bound functions benefit most from more memory
- I/O-bound functions (waiting on network) don't benefit much past 1 vCPU

## Cost Optimization

### Compute

| Strategy | Savings | Applies To |
|---|---|---|
| ARM64 (Graviton2) | 20% | All Lambda functions |
| Right-size memory | 10-50% | Over-provisioned functions |
| Savings Plans | Up to 17% | Predictable workloads |
| Shorter timeout | Prevents runaway costs | All functions |

### API Gateway

| Strategy | Savings |
|---|---|
| HTTP API instead of REST API | 71% ($1 vs $3.50 per 1M) |
| Caching (REST API only) | Reduces backend invocations |
| Request validation | Rejects bad requests before Lambda |

### DynamoDB

| Strategy | Savings |
|---|---|
| On-demand for variable traffic | No over-provisioning |
| Reserved capacity for steady traffic | Up to 77% |
| TTL for ephemeral data | Reduces storage costs |
| Sparse GSIs | Only index items that need it |

### Data Transfer

| Strategy | Savings |
|---|---|
| VPC endpoints (gateway) for S3/DynamoDB | Free (vs NAT Gateway $0.045/GB) |
| CloudFront for API caching | Reduces origin requests |
| Single-AZ for dev | Eliminates cross-AZ transfer |
| Compress responses | Reduces transfer volume |

## Concurrency Management

### Account-Level

A person's commands (they need the account):

```bash
# Check current limit
aws lambda get-account-settings --query 'AccountLimit.ConcurrentExecutions'

# Request increase via Service Quotas
aws service-quotas request-service-quota-increase \
  --service-code lambda \
  --quota-code L-B99A9384 \
  --desired-value 3000
```

### Function-Level

```typescript
// CDK: Reserved concurrency (hard limit)
handler.addAlias('live', {
  provisionedConcurrentExecutions: 10,  // Pre-warmed
});

// Reserved concurrency (max concurrent)
new CfnFunction(this, 'Config', {
  reservedConcurrentExecutions: 100,
});
```

**Rules:**
- Reserved concurrency = max concurrent executions for this function
- Provisioned concurrency = pre-warmed environments (eliminates cold starts)
- Sum of all reserved concurrency must be < account limit
- Unreserved functions share remaining pool

## Streaming Responses

```typescript
// Lambda response streaming (reduces TTFB)
export const handler = awslambda.streamifyResponse(
  async (event, responseStream, context) => {
    responseStream.write('Starting...\n');
    for (const item of items) {
      const result = await process(item);
      responseStream.write(JSON.stringify(result) + '\n');
    }
    responseStream.end();
  }
);
```

**When to use:**
- Large responses (>6MB sync limit, up to 200MB streamed)
- Time-to-first-byte matters (chat, real-time)
- Progressive rendering

## Performance Monitoring

### Key Metrics

| Metric | What It Tells You | Action Threshold |
|---|---|---|
| Duration (p50/p99) | Execution time distribution | p99 > 80% of timeout |
| ColdStartDuration | Init time | > 1s for user-facing |
| ConcurrentExecutions | Current usage | > 80% of limit |
| Throttles | Hitting concurrency limit | > 0 |
| IteratorAge | Stream consumer lag | > 60s |
| Errors | Function failures | > 1% |

### CloudWatch Insights Queries

```
# Top 10 slowest invocations
fields @timestamp, @duration, @requestId
| filter @type = "REPORT"
| sort @duration desc
| limit 10

# Cold start frequency
fields @timestamp, @initDuration
| filter ispresent(@initDuration)
| stats count() as coldStarts, avg(@initDuration) as avgInit by bin(1h)

# Error patterns
fields @timestamp, @message
| filter @message like /ERROR/
| stats count() by @message
| sort count desc
| limit 10
```

| Claim | Source | Checked |
|---|---|---|
| Lambda Durable Functions GA, checkpoint/resume via `context.step()`/`context.wait()`, pause up to 1 year, US East (Ohio) only, Python 3.13/3.14 + Node.js 22/24 | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/durable-functions.html, https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2025/12/lambda-durable-multi-step-applications-ai-workflows/ | 2026-10-28 |
| SnapStart supports Java 11+, Python 3.12+, .NET 8+ (not Java-only) | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/snapstart.html, https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/aws/aws-lambda-snapstart-for-python-and-net-functions-is-now-generally-available/ | 2026-10-28 |
| `NodejsFunction.logRetention` is deprecated in favor of `logGroup` | https://constructs.dev/packages/aws-cdk-lib/v/2.275.0/api/NodejsFunction | 2026-10-28 |
| HTTP API $1.00/M (first 300M)/mo vs REST API $3.50/M (first 333M)/mo | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/best-practices-api-gateway-private-apis-integration/cost-optimization.html | 2026-10-28 |

---
name: cdk-doctor
description: "Diagnoses failed AWS CDK or CloudFormation deployments and crashing ECS tasks from the error text, and validates infrastructure changes offline: failure patterns, Fargate sizes, AMI and image choice. Read it when a task quotes a deploy failure or before submitting an IaC change."
source: "ai-skill-factory 2.0.0 (Amit Deol), skills/cdk-doctor"
license: MIT
adapted: "The agents have no AWS account and never deploy: diagnosis starts from the error text the task or issue quotes (stopped reasons, stack events, target health), the AWS CLI commands became what to ask a person for, and the deploy-and-monitor and post-deployment steps (with the monitor sub-agent) are dropped. Validation is offline (synth, cfn-lint, nag, guard). Slash references name library skills; the GPU skill reference is dropped; description and emphasis reworded for Claude 5.5 skill discovery"
---

Diagnose the CDK deployment failure your task names, and fix it in code.

Debugging skill. For writing or restructuring CDK code, use the `cdk-engineer` skill, which owns the construct
ladder, version pinning, and escape hatches. Root-cause method: the `systematic-debugging` skill.

You have no AWS account and the run never deploys. The evidence is what your task and the run's issue quote: the
CloudFormation events, an ECS stopped reason, a target's health reason, a log line. Match it against the tables
below, fix the cause in the code, validate offline (Step 1), and say in your finish what a person should check
after they deploy. When the evidence is missing, `finish` naming the exact command output you need (the commands
are below), rather than guess.

## Step 1: Pre-Deployment Validation (offline)

Catches most failures before anyone deploys.

| Check | Command | Catches |
|---|---|---|
| Synthesize | `cdk synth` | Import errors, construct issues, asset bundling |
| Template lint | `cfn-lint` on each template under `cdk.out/` | Invalid properties, missing required fields |
| CDK-nag | Add `Aspects.of(app).add(new AwsSolutionsChecks());` and run `cdk synth` | IAM over-permissions, missing encryption, unencrypted logs at synthesis time |
| Policy guard | `cfn-guard validate --data template.json --rules policy.guard` | Compliance violations |

`cdk diff` needs the deployed account: a person runs it before they deploy, and your test of the stateful
resources' logical IDs (the `cdk-engineer` skill, Step 6) stands in for its replacement check.

### Fargate CPU/Memory Validation

Fargate rejects invalid combinations at registration time. Validate BEFORE deploying:

| CPU (units) | Valid Memory (MiB) | OS |
|---|---|---|
| 256 (.25 vCPU) | 512, 1024, 2048 | Linux |
| 512 (.5 vCPU) | 1024-4096 (1 GB increments) | Linux |
| 1024 (1 vCPU) | 2048-8192 (1 GB increments) | Linux, Windows |
| 2048 (2 vCPU) | 4096-16384 (1 GB increments) | Linux, Windows |
| 4096 (4 vCPU) | 8192-30720 (1 GB increments) | Linux, Windows |
| 8192 (8 vCPU) | 16384-61440 (4 GB increments) | Linux, platform 1.4.0+ |
| 16384 (16 vCPU) | 32768-122880 (8 GB increments) | Linux, platform 1.4.0+ |

Container memory sum must not exceed task-level memory. Full table:
[ECS task definition parameters for Fargate](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/task_definition_parameters.html).

### Pre-Deploy Checklist

- [ ] Stateful resources' logical IDs asserted unchanged (a person's `cdk diff` shows no replacement)
- [ ] ECS task def: CPU/memory combo is valid for Fargate
- [ ] Security groups allow traffic between ALB and containers
- [ ] VPC has NAT gateway or VPC endpoints for ECR access (private subnets)
- [ ] IAM task role has permissions for all AWS services the container calls
- [ ] Container health check endpoint returns 200
- [ ] Environment variables and secrets configured
- [ ] `env: { account, region }` set on stacks (prevents cross-region failures)

## Step 2: ECS Debugging

When ECS tasks fail, the stopped reason comes FIRST. These are the commands a person runs to get it (name them in
your finish when the issue does not quote their output):

```bash
# Find failed tasks
aws ecs list-tasks --cluster CLUSTER --desired-status STOPPED --query 'taskArns[0:5]'

# Get stopped reason
aws ecs describe-tasks --cluster CLUSTER --tasks TASK_ARN \
  --query 'tasks[0].[stoppedReason,stopCode,containers[0].reason]'
```

### ECS Failure Pattern → Fix

| Stopped Reason | Root Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `CannotPullContainerError` | ECR unreachable (no NAT/VPC endpoint) or image missing | Add NAT gateway or ECR VPC endpoint; verify image tag exists |
| `OutOfMemoryError` | Container exceeded task memory | Increase task memory or optimize container |
| `Task failed ELB health checks` | Health check endpoint not returning 200 | Fix health check path, increase deregistration delay |
| `ResourceNotFoundException` | Secrets Manager/SSM parameter missing | Create the secret/parameter before deploying |
| `unable to place task` | No instances with enough CPU/memory | Increase desired capacity or use larger instance type |
| `EssentialContainerExited` | Application crashed on startup | Check CloudWatch Logs for container stdout/stderr |

### CloudWatch Logs (a person's commands)

```bash
# Get log group from task definition
aws ecs describe-task-definition --task-definition TASK_DEF \
  --query 'taskDefinition.containerDefinitions[0].logConfiguration.options."awslogs-group"'

# Read recent logs
aws logs filter-log-events --log-group-name LOG_GROUP \
  --filter-pattern "ERROR" --limit 20 \
  --query 'events[*].[timestamp,message]'
```

### ALB Target Health (a person's commands)

```bash
aws elbv2 describe-target-health --target-group-arn TG_ARN \
  --query 'TargetHealthDescriptions[*].[Target.Id,TargetHealth.State,TargetHealth.Reason,TargetHealth.Description]'
```

| Health Reason | Meaning | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `Target.ResponseCodeMismatch` | Container returns wrong status code | Fix health check path or expected codes |
| `Target.Timeout` | Container not responding in time | Increase timeout or fix slow startup |
| `Target.FailedHealthChecks` | Consecutive failures exceeded threshold | Check security groups, container port |
| `Elb.InternalError` | ALB issue | Check ALB logs, security groups |

## Step 3: AMI and Image Intelligence

### AMI Discovery via SSM

| AMI Type | SSM Parameter Path |
|---|---|
| Amazon Linux 2023 | `/aws/service/ami-amazon-linux-latest/al2023-ami-kernel-default-x86_64` |
| ECS-optimized (AL2) | `/aws/service/ecs/optimized-ami/amazon-linux-2/recommended` |
| ECS-optimized (AL2023) | `/aws/service/ecs/optimized-ami/amazon-linux-2023/recommended` |
| ECS GPU-optimized | `/aws/service/ecs/optimized-ami/amazon-linux-2/gpu/recommended` |
| EKS-optimized | `/aws/service/eks/optimized-ami/{k8s-version}/amazon-linux-2/recommended` |

Resolving a parameter needs the account: in code, resolve it at synth with `cachedInContext` (below), whose value
`cdk.context.json` records.

### CDK AMI Patterns

```typescript
// Resolve via SSM. Without cachedInContext the parameter is re-read every deployment,
// which replaces your instances whenever a new AMI ships.
ec2.MachineImage.fromSsmParameter(
  '/aws/service/ecs/optimized-ami/amazon-linux-2/recommended',
  { cachedInContext: true },   // records the AMI ID in cdk.context.json
);

// Pin to specific AMI (for reproducibility)
ec2.MachineImage.genericLinux({ 'us-east-1': 'ami-0c55b159cbfafe1f0' });
```

### Version-First Principle

Before installing any software on an instance or container:
1. Check what the base AMI/image already includes
2. Only upgrade if the existing version is incompatible
3. Pin versions in Dockerfile/user data to prevent drift

Full AMI inspection, CUDA/GPU compatibility, container image patterns: `references/ami-intelligence.md`.

## Step 4: Common CloudFormation Failures

| Error Pattern | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `Circular dependency` | Resources reference each other | Break cycle with explicit security group ingress rules |
| `Export EXPORT_NAME cannot be deleted` | Another stack imports this export | Update importing stack first |
| `Resource limit exceeded` | Hit account service quota | Request quota increase |
| `UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED` | Rollback itself failed | A person runs `aws cloudformation continue-update-rollback --stack-name STACK`; no code change fixes it |
| `The security token included in the request is invalid` | Expired credentials | The deploying person's credentials; no code change fixes it |

## Step 5: What to Hand Back

Your `finish` says: the cause, matched to its evidence; the code change; the offline checks and their exit codes;
and what a person checks after they deploy (the ECS service's running count against its desired count, the
targets' health, the log group's errors in the minutes after).

For IAM and security policy validation, see the `aws-security` skill. For AMI and container image selection, see
`references/ami-intelligence.md`. For Docker build and image hardening, see the `docker-ops` skill.

references.text:
# AMI and Container Image Intelligence

## Version-First Principle

Before installing any software: check what the base AMI/image already includes. Only upgrade if incompatible.

## Deep Learning AMI (DLAMI) Contents

AWS DLAMIs pre-install multiple framework versions in isolated Conda environments:

| Component | Typical Versions | Check command (on the instance: a person's check) |
|---|---|---|
| CUDA Toolkit | 11.8, 12.1, 12.4 | `ls /usr/local/cuda*` |
| cuDNN | Matching CUDA versions | `cat /usr/local/cuda/include/cudnn_version.h` |
| NCCL | Multi-GPU communication | `dpkg -l | grep nccl` |
| PyTorch | Pre-compiled for CUDA | `conda activate pytorch && python -c "import torch; print(torch.__version__)"` |
| TensorFlow | Pre-compiled for CUDA | `conda activate tensorflow && python -c "import tensorflow; print(tensorflow.__version__)"` |
| Python | 3.10, 3.11, 3.12 | `python3 --version` |
| NVIDIA driver | 535+, 550+ | `nvidia-smi` |

## CUDA/GPU Compatibility

### Instance Type → GPU

| Instance Type | GPU | Compute Capability | Use Case |
|---|---|---|---|
| g4dn.* | T4 | 7.5 (Turing) | Inference, light training |
| g5.* | A10G | 8.6 (Ampere) | Training, inference |
| p4d.24xlarge | A100 | 8.0 (Ampere) | Large-scale training |
| p5.48xlarge | H100 | 9.0 (Hopper) | LLM training |
| g6.* | L4 | 8.9 (Ada) | Inference |

### CUDA → Framework Compatibility

| CUDA | Min Driver | PyTorch | TensorFlow | Triton | FlashInfer |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 12.4 | 550.54+ | 2.2+ | 2.16+ | 3.5+ | 0.5+ |
| 12.1 | 530.30+ | 2.1+ | 2.14+ | 3.0+ | 0.4+ |
| 11.8 | 520.61+ | 2.0+ | 2.12+ | 2.0+ | 0.3+ |

### Version Check Before Upgrading

```bash
# What CUDA is installed?
nvcc --version
nvidia-smi  # shows driver version and max CUDA supported

# What PyTorch expects
python3 -c "import torch; print(torch.version.cuda)"

# What FlashInfer needs
python3 -c "import flashinfer; flashinfer.show_config()" 2>/dev/null || echo "Not installed"
```

**Decision rule**: If the installed CUDA version satisfies your framework's minimum, do not upgrade, because CUDA upgrades risk breaking other pre-installed frameworks.

## Container Base Image Selection

### Python ML Images

| Image | Size | Pre-installed | Best For |
|---|---|---|---|
| `python:3.12-slim` | ~150 MB | Python only | API services, no ML |
| `nvidia/cuda:12.1.0-runtime-ubuntu22.04` | ~3 GB | CUDA runtime | Inference with custom deps |
| `nvidia/cuda:12.1.0-devel-ubuntu22.04` | ~5 GB | CUDA + compiler | Building from source |
| AWS DL Container (ECR public) | ~8 GB | CUDA + PyTorch/TF | Full ML stack |

### Inspecting an Image

Image metadata (tags, sizes) lives in its registry, which the sandbox cannot reach. Choose a base image from what
the repository already pins and from the table above, name the tag and the reason in your finish, and leave a
registry check (ECR Public, Docker Hub) to a person.

## ECS-Optimized AMI Contents

| Component | Version (typical) | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Amazon Linux 2 / AL2023 | Latest | Auto-updated via SSM |
| Docker | 20.10+ / 25+ | Managed by ECS agent |
| ECS agent | Latest | Auto-updated |
| nvidia-container-runtime | Included in GPU AMI | Required for GPU tasks |

### GPU ECS Setup Checklist

- [ ] Use ECS GPU-optimized AMI (SSM: `/aws/service/ecs/optimized-ami/amazon-linux-2/gpu/recommended`)
- [ ] Instance type has GPU (g4dn, g5, p4d, p5)
- [ ] Task definition specifies GPU resource requirements
- [ ] Container has NVIDIA runtime configured
- [ ] CUDA version in container matches driver on host

# Sources

Non-obvious claims in this skill, with the source checked and the date checked.

| Claim | Source | Checked |
|---|---|---|
| Fargate CPU/memory valid combinations, including 8192/16384 vCPU tiers requiring platform 1.4.0+ | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/task_definition_parameters.html | 2026-10-28 |
| AL2023 SSM parameter path `/aws/service/ami-amazon-linux-latest/al2023-ami-kernel-default-x86_64` | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/linux/al2023/ug/ec2.html | 2026-10-28 |
| cdk-nag `AwsSolutionsChecks` Aspect usage | https://github.com/cdklabs/cdk-nag/tree/main/README.md | 2026-10-28 |

adapted: "The spec-loader step reads INFRA.md and STANDARDS.md with read_file. Versions come from the repository's lockfile, not a registry query (no network). The gate is offline: synth, nag, cfn-lint and tests; cdk diff and deploy need an account the agents never have, and a person deploys. Commands are run's argv. Slash references name library skills; description reworded for Claude 5.5 skill discovery"
---

Model the infrastructure your task asks for in CDK, at the highest construct level that fits.

Authoring skill. For a failed `cdk deploy`, use the `cdk-doctor` skill. For IAM and encryption policy, the
`aws-security` skill. For the general no-hand-rolling ladder, the `use-the-sdk` skill.

The run never deploys: you write and test the CDK code, offline, and a person deploys it.

## Step 0: Load Project Standards

If the repository has an INFRA.md, read it with `read_file` for approved services, regions and account layout,
and a STANDARDS.md for language, package manager and size limits; else the defaults below. Read `cdk.json` for
context, feature flags, and the app entry point.

## Step 1: Take Versions From the Repository

Never recall a version from memory. Read what the repository pins: `package.json` and its lockfile (or
`requirements.txt`, `pyproject.toml` and its lock) for `aws-cdk-lib`, `constructs`, `aws-cdk` and `cdk-nag`, and the
installed copy under `node_modules/` (or the virtual environment). The sandbox has no network, so a registry query
(`npm view`, PyPI) is not possible: a newer version you believe exists is named in your finish as unchecked, never
written into a pin.

Anchor, verified 28 October 2026 (for orientation only; the repository's pins win):

| Package | Version |
|---|---|
| `aws-cdk-lib` | 2.275.0 |
| `aws-cdk` (CLI) | 2.1146.1 |
| `constructs` | 10.8.1 |
| `cdk-nag` | 3.0.2 |

Rules: one `aws-cdk-lib` entry, never per-service v1 packages. `constructs` on `^10`.
Alpha modules carry their own `-alpha.N` version that must match the `aws-cdk-lib` minor.
If the repo is more than a few minors behind and the code needs a newer construct, say so
rather than reimplementing the construct by hand.

## Step 2: The Construct Ladder

Stop at the first rung that satisfies the requirement. Record the rung in the report.

| # | Rung | Example |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Existing construct in this repo | Search `lib/` and `constructs/` before writing anything |
| 2 | L3 pattern | `ApplicationLoadBalancedFargateService`, `LambdaRestApi`, AWS Solutions Constructs, Construct Hub |
| 3 | L2 construct | `Bucket`, `Table`, `Function`, `StateMachine`, `Queue`, `Vpc` |
| 4 | L2 plus escape hatch | `addPropertyOverride` on the L2's `defaultChild` for a missing property |
| 5 | L1 `Cfn*` resource | Only when no L2 exists for that resource type |
| 6 | Custom resource | `AwsCustomResource`, or the provider framework for multi-step work |
| 7 | Hand-written code | Effectively never. Justify it in the report |

Rung 4 is the one that gets skipped. A missing property is not a reason to drop the whole
resource to L1, which forfeits every grant, metric, and sane default the L2 provides.

```typescript
const cfnBucket = bucket.node.defaultChild as s3.CfnBucket;
cfnBucket.addPropertyOverride("AccelerateConfiguration.AccelerationStatus", "Enabled");
```

Escape hatch techniques, including `addOverride`, `addDeletionOverride`, raw overrides, and
removing generated resources: `references/escape-hatches.md`.

## Step 3: Structural Rules

From the official [CDK best practices](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cdk/v2/guide/best-practices.html).
These prevent rework that no amount of clean construct code recovers from.

| Rule | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| Model with constructs, deploy with stacks | A logical unit is a `Construct`. Stacks only describe how units compose for a deployment scenario |
| Configure with props and methods, not environment variables | Env lookups inside a construct bind it to the machine. Confine them to the app entry point |
| Decide at synthesis time | Use the language's `if` and loops. Avoid `CfnParameter`, `CfnCondition`, and `Fn::If` |
| Model every stage in code | A stack per stage with its config in source, not one parameterised template |
| Let CDK generate physical names | A hardcoded `bucketName` or `tableName` blocks a second deployment and blocks replacement |
| Split stateful from stateless stacks | Turn on termination protection for the stateful stack, then redeploy stateless freely |
| Never change the logical ID of a stateful resource | Renaming or re-parenting replaces it. Assert IDs in a test (Step 6) |
| Set removal policy and log retention deliberately | CDK defaults retain data and logs forever, which becomes a cost problem in production |
| No side effects or network lookups during synth | Synth must be deterministic. Commit `cdk.context.json` so `fromLookup` results are stable |

Constructs alone are not compliance. A `MyCompanyBucket` wrapper surfaces guidance early, but
enforcement belongs in service control policies, permission boundaries, Aspects, and
cfn-guard. A wrapper also blocks consumers from AWS Solutions Constructs and Construct Hub.

Detail and worked examples: `references/app-structure.md`.

## Step 4: Never Hand-Roll These in CDK

Each is a MUST finding. Use the named built-in.

| Hand-rolled | Use instead |
|---|---|
| IAM policy JSON or `PolicyStatement` for a common flow | `grantRead`, `grantWrite`, `grantInvoke`, `grantPutEvents` |
| ARN built by string concatenation or template literal | Resource attribute (`table.tableArn`), or `Arn.format` / `stack.formatArn` |
| Region, account, or partition hardcoded | `Stack.of(this).region`, `.account`, `.partition` |
| Custom log-retention Lambda | `logRetention` or `logGroup` on the L2 |
| CloudWatch alarm built from raw metric namespaces | `resource.metricXxx().createAlarm()` |
| Hand-written subnet CIDR maths | `Vpc` with `ipAddresses` and `subnetConfiguration` |
| Cross-stack value passed as a string export | Pass the construct or its typed attribute |
| Secret value read into a variable | `Secret.fromSecretNameV2`, `secret.grantRead`, `ecs.Secret.fromSecretsManager` |
| Bundling shelled out through `local-exec` style commands | `NodejsFunction`, `PythonFunction`, `Code.fromAssetImage`, `DockerImageAsset` |
| Environment variable read inside a construct or stack | A props object. Confine env and context reads to the app entry point |
| Physical resource name hardcoded to make a reference work | Pass `table.tableName` as an env var, or read it from SSM at runtime |
| Polling loop waiting for a resource | Custom resource provider framework `isComplete`, or a Step Functions wait |
| Tags applied per resource | `Tags.of(scope).add(...)` at stack or app scope |
| Hand-built Step Functions state JSON | `aws-cdk-lib/aws-stepfunctions-tasks` classes |
| Manual `DependsOn` string wiring | `resource.node.addDependency(other)` |
| String manipulation on a token | `Fn.select`, `Fn.split`, `Token.asString`, `Lazy.string` |

`grant*` methods are the single most-missed built-in. They write a least-privilege policy and
attach any needed KMS grant. A hand-written statement usually misses the KMS half.

## Step 5: Verify the API Before Using It

The most common CDK defect from an agent is a plausible property that does not exist. Before
first use of any construct, prop, or method:

- `list_files` on `node_modules/aws-cdk-lib/aws-lambda/lib/`, then `read_file` on its `.d.ts` files
- `run` `["grep", "-rn", "readonly memorySize", "node_modules/aws-cdk-lib/aws-lambda/lib/function-props.d.ts"]`
- Python apps: `run` `["python3", "-c", "import aws_cdk.aws_lambda as l; help(l.FunctionProps)"]`

Read the installed source, not your recollection. If a symbol is absent from the installed
version, either upgrade deliberately or use the escape hatch. Do not invent a prop name.
Protocol: the `code-review` skill's api-verification reference.

## Step 6: Tests Before Anyone Deploys

Fine-grained assertions catch what `synth` alone does not.

```typescript
const template = Template.fromStack(stack);
template.hasResourceProperties("AWS::S3::Bucket", {
  BucketEncryption: Match.objectLike({ ServerSideEncryptionConfiguration: Match.anyValue() }),
});
template.resourceCountIs("AWS::IAM::Role", 2);
```

- Assert on the properties that carry policy: encryption, retention, public access, removal.
- Assert that the logical IDs of stateful resources are unchanged, so a later refactor cannot
  silently replace a database or bucket. This is the cheapest test in the suite.
- Snapshot tests catch drift. Review the snapshot diff, do not accept it blindly (the `tdd` skill, Step 6).
- Test synth for both dev and prod context values when behaviour branches on context.

```typescript
expect(Object.keys(template.findResources("AWS::DynamoDB::Table"))).toEqual(["OrdersTableABC12345"]);
```

## Step 7: Gate Before Reporting Done

| Gate | Command | Blocks on |
|---|---|---|
| Synth | `cdk synth` (offline: a `fromLookup` the committed `cdk.context.json` does not answer fails here) | Construct and import errors |
| Nag | cdk-nag `AwsSolutionsChecks` as an Aspect | Security rule violations, unjustified suppressions |
| Lint | `cfn-lint` on each template under `cdk.out/` | Invalid property values |
| Tests | `npm test` / `python -m pytest` | Assertion failures |

`cdk diff` and `cdk deploy` need the deployed account, which an agent never has: the logical-ID assertions of
Step 6 stand in for the diff's replacement check, and your finish says the diff is a person's to read before they
deploy. Every cdk-nag suppression needs a reason string naming the compensating control. A blanket suppression is a
MUST finding. Deployment failures after this point: the `cdk-doctor` skill.

## Step 8: Report

Put this in your `finish` summary:

```
## CDK: [what was modelled]

| Resource | Rung | Construct | Rejected |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fargate service | 2 (L3) | ApplicationLoadBalancedFargateService | 40 lines of L1 + LB wiring |
| S3 accelerate | 4 (escape hatch) | Bucket + addPropertyOverride | full L1 CfnBucket |

- Versions: aws-cdk-lib X (from the lockfile), CLI Y
- Built-ins used: grantRead, metricErrors, logRetention
- API verified: [symbol, file read]
- Gates: synth exit 0, nag 0 unsuppressed, logical IDs asserted, tests X passed; cdk diff left to a person
- Suppressions: [rule, reason, compensating control]
```

## Self-Check

- [ ] Versions taken from the repository's pins, not recalled
- [ ] Highest workable rung chosen, and the rung recorded
- [ ] No L1 resource where an L2 exists, no L1 drop to reach one property
- [ ] No item from the Step 3 table hand-rolled
- [ ] Every prop and method confirmed against installed source
- [ ] `grant*` used instead of hand-written policy statements
- [ ] Step 3 structural rules held: constructs for modelling, props for config, synth-time decisions
- [ ] No physical names hardcoded, no logical ID change on a stateful resource
- [ ] Removal policy and log retention chosen deliberately for production resources
- [ ] `cdk.context.json` answers every `fromLookup` (a lookup needs the account; you have none)
- [ ] Logical IDs of stateful resources asserted, so a person's cdk diff shows no replacement
- [ ] Nag suppressions justified individually

Before you claim the stack works, apply the `verification-before-completion` skill.

# CDK App Structure and Determinism

Detail behind Step 3 of the `cdk-engineer` skill. Sourced from the official
[AWS CDK best practices](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cdk/v2/guide/best-practices.html) and the
[CDK layer guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/aws-cdk-layers/best-practices.html),
read 28 October 2026.

## Model With Constructs, Deploy With Stacks

A stack is the unit of deployment: everything in it deploys together. A logical unit of your
system is therefore a `Construct`, not a `Stack`.

```typescript
// The website is a construct: bucket, distribution, API, functions.
export class Website extends Construct { /* ... */ }

// Stacks only describe composition for a deployment scenario.
class ProdStack extends Stack {
  constructor(scope: Construct, id: string, props: StackProps) {
    super(scope, id, props);
    new Website(this, "Website", { domain: "example.com", minCapacity: 4 });
  }
}
```

Modelling a logical unit as a `Stack` forfeits reuse and forces deployment shape onto design.

## Configure With Props, Not Environment Variables

An env lookup inside a construct binds it to whichever machine runs synth, which is untracked
configuration. Accept a props object instead.

```typescript
// Wrong: the construct now depends on the shell that synthesised it.
const tableName = process.env.TABLE_NAME;

// Right: the caller decides, and the type system checks it.
interface ApiProps { readonly table: dynamodb.ITable; }
```

Confine env and context reads to the app entry point, and only for development-time values.

## Decide at Synthesis Time

CloudFormation `Parameters`, `Conditions`, and `Fn::If` push decisions to deploy time, where the
available types and operations are far narrower than a programming language. They also break
determinism: the same template can produce different infrastructure.

| Instead of | Use |
|---|---|
| `CfnParameter` for an environment name | A separate stack per stage, config in code |
| `CfnCondition` around a resource | An `if` in the construct, or a different stack |
| `Fn::If` to pick a size | A value from props, chosen by the calling stack |

Treat CloudFormation as an implementation detail, not a language target.

## Model Every Stage in Code

One stack per stage, each with its configuration in source. Sensitive values come from Secrets
Manager or Parameter Store by name or ARN, not from a checked-in literal. Synth then produces a
separate deterministic template per environment in `cdk.out`, which makes unit tests meaningful.

## Let CDK Generate Physical Names

A name can only be used once per account and region. Hardcoding `bucketName` or `tableName`:

- Blocks a second deployment of the same stack into one account.
- Blocks any change that requires replacement, because the replacement cannot take a name the
  original still holds. Immutable properties such as a DynamoDB `KeySchema` require replacement.

Pass the generated name where it is needed instead: an env var on a Lambda function, an SSM
parameter the application reads, or a construct reference between stacks in the same app. For
a resource in a different app, use a `from*` static method with the ARN.

## Stateful and Stateless Stacks

Keep databases, buckets, and VPCs in a separate stack from compute:

- Turn on termination protection for the stateful stack.
- Destroy and recreate the stateless stack freely, including per-developer copies.
- Stateful resources are the most sensitive to renaming, so keep them out of constructs that
  are likely to be moved or restructured.

## Logical IDs and Replacement

A logical ID derives from the construct id and its position in the tree. Renaming either
replaces the resource. For a database or bucket that means data loss or an orphaned resource.

- Assert stateful logical IDs in a unit test, so a refactor fails the build rather than the
  deployment.
- To restructure while keeping a resource, pin the old value with `overrideLogicalId`.
- Before anyone deploys a restructure, `cdk diff` must show zero replacements (a person reads it: the agents have
  no account).

## Removal Policy and Log Retention

CDK defaults protect data: resources holding data are orphaned rather than deleted, and logs
are retained forever. Both defaults cost money in production if left unexamined.

| Resource | Decide |
|---|---|
| Data stores | `removalPolicy`: retain for production, destroy for ephemeral dev stacks |
| Log groups | `retention`: a real period, not the default indefinite |
| Snapshots | Whether a final snapshot is taken on delete |

Validate these with an Aspect so the rule applies to every resource, not the ones you remembered.

## Determinism and cdk.context.json

Synth must produce the same template for the same commit. Two failure modes:

- A `fromLookup` or SDK call at synth time returns a different value later. The classic cases
  are the AZ count changing, which re-splits your CIDR space, and a new AMI being released,
  which replaces every instance.
- Synth mutates the account. Synth must have no side effects, so changes belong in the deploy
  phase where CloudFormation can roll them back. Use a custom resource for deploy-time work.

Context providers cache lookup results in `cdk.context.json`. Commit it. Refresh entries
deliberately with the CDK CLI context commands. For a value with no context provider, write a
separate script that records it to a file, and run that script only when you intend to refresh.

## Compliance Needs More Than Constructs

Wrapping an L2 to bake in encryption and IAM defaults is useful for surfacing guidance early.
It is not enforcement, and it has a cost.

| Layer | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| Prevention at the org level | Service control policies, permission boundaries |
| Assertion before deployment | Aspects, cdk-nag, cfn-guard |
| Guidance at authoring time | Wrapper constructs, shared construct library |

A private wrapper also blocks consumers from AWS Solutions Constructs, Construct Hub, and
third-party constructs, since those build on the standard L2s. Weigh that before mandating one.

# CDK Escape Hatches

Rung 4 of the construct ladder in the `cdk-engineer` skill. Reach for these when an L2 construct lacks a
property, so you keep its grants, metrics, and defaults instead of dropping to L1.

Verified against `aws-cdk-lib` 2.275.0, 28 October 2026.

## Getting the L1 Behind an L2

```typescript
const cfnBucket = bucket.node.defaultChild as s3.CfnBucket;
```

```python
cfn_bucket = bucket.node.default_child  # type: s3.CfnBucket
```

For a construct whose L1 is nested deeper, walk the tree rather than guessing:

```typescript
stack.node.findAll().forEach((c) => console.log(c.node.path, c.constructor.name));
```

## The Four Override Methods

| Method | Use for | Note |
|---|---|---|
| `addPropertyOverride(path, value)` | A property CloudFormation supports and the L2 does not expose | Path uses CloudFormation property names, dot separated |
| `addOverride(path, value)` | Anything outside `Properties`, such as `UpdatePolicy` or `Metadata` | Prefix a resource-level path with no `Properties.` |
| `addDeletionOverride(path)` | Removing a property the L2 sets that you do not want | Safer than setting it to undefined |
| `addPropertyDeletionOverride(path)` | Removing one generated property | Scoped to `Properties` |

```typescript
cfnBucket.addPropertyOverride("AccelerateConfiguration.AccelerationStatus", "Enabled");
cfnBucket.addOverride("UpdateReplacePolicy", "Retain");
cfnBucket.addDeletionOverride("Properties.LoggingConfiguration");
```

Escaped hatch values bypass CDK validation. Confirm the property name and casing against the
CloudFormation resource reference for that resource type before using it.

## Path Casing: Match the CloudFormation Schema, Not the L2 Prop

`addPropertyOverride` and `addOverride` take a dot-separated path into the rendered
CloudFormation template, not the L2's TypeScript/Python prop name. The path must use the exact
CloudFormation property names (PascalCase), including list indices:

```typescript
cfnBucket.addPropertyOverride("Tags.0.Value", "NewValue");         // CFN property name, not `tags`
cfnBucket.addPropertyOverride("VersioningConfiguration.Status", "Enabled");
```

There is no `addRawOverride` method on `CfnResource`; it does not exist in `aws-cdk-lib`. If a
path write does not take effect, the cause is almost always a mismatched CloudFormation property
name or an index into the wrong list depth. Check the
[CloudFormation resource reference](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/UserGuide/aws-template-resource-type-ref.html)
for the exact property name before adjusting the path.

## Escaping Upward: Wrapping an L1 as an L2

When no L2 exists at all, write a small construct that owns the L1 and exposes typed
attributes and `grant*` methods. This is a legitimate custom construct, not hand-rolling,
because it concentrates the raw resource behind one reviewed boundary.

```typescript
export class Thing extends Construct {
  public readonly arn: string;
  constructor(scope: Construct, id: string, props: ThingProps) {
    super(scope, id);
    const resource = new svc.CfnThing(this, "Resource", { ... });
    this.arn = resource.attrArn;
  }
  public grantRead(grantee: iam.IGrantable) {
    return iam.Grant.addToPrincipal({ grantee, actions: ["svc:GetThing"], resourceArns: [this.arn] });
  }
}
```

Do not scatter `Cfn*` resources across stacks. One wrapper, reviewed once.

## Removing a Generated Resource

Occasionally an L2 creates a resource you must not have, such as an auto-generated log group
already managed elsewhere:

```typescript
const child = construct.node.tryFindChild("LogRetention") as cdk.CfnResource | undefined;
child?.node.scope?.node.tryRemoveChild("LogRetention");
```

Prefer configuring the L2 to not create it. Removal is a last resort, and `cdk diff` must be
read carefully afterwards, since removing a resource from the template can delete it.

## Logical ID Stability

Escape hatches do not change logical IDs. Renaming or re-parenting a construct does, which
replaces the resource. To keep an existing resource while restructuring:

```typescript
cfnBucket.overrideLogicalId("MyOriginalBucketLogicalId1234ABCD");
```

Before anyone deploys a restructure, `cdk diff` must show zero replacements. The diff needs the deployed
account, which the agents never have: assert the stateful logical IDs in a test, and say in your finish that the
diff is the deploying person's to read. A replacement on a stateful resource (bucket, table, database) is a MUST
finding unless intended and backed up.

## When an Escape Hatch Is the Wrong Answer

| Situation | Do this instead |
|---|---|
| The property exists on the L2 under a different name | Use the real prop. Verify against installed source |
| You need behaviour, not configuration | Custom resource provider framework |
| The resource type has no L2 and you need it in several places | Wrap the L1 in a construct, as above |
| A newer `aws-cdk-lib` exposes the property | Upgrade deliberately, and say so |
| The requirement is a security control | Model it properly, then let cdk-nag check it (the `aws-security` skill) |

# Sources

Non-obvious claims in this skill, with the source checked and the date checked.

| Claim | Source | Checked |
|---|---|---|
| `aws-cdk-lib` 2.275.0, `aws-cdk` CLI 2.1146.1, `constructs` 10.8.1, `cdk-nag` 3.0.2 | https://registry.npmjs.org/aws-cdk-lib/latest, /aws-cdk/latest, /constructs/latest, /cdk-nag/latest | 2026-10-28 |
| `CfnResource` has `addOverride`, `addPropertyOverride`, `addDeletionOverride`, `addPropertyDeletionOverride`; no `addRawOverride` method exists | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cdk/v2/guide/cfn-layer.md | 2026-10-28 |
| Override paths use CloudFormation property names (PascalCase), not the L2 TypeScript/Python prop name | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cdk/v2/guide/cfn-layer.md | 2026-10-28 |
| CDK structural best practices (constructs vs stacks, props over env vars, synth-time decisions, physical names, logical ID stability) | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cdk/v2/guide/best-practices.html | 2026-10-28 |
