library.text:
---
name: cicd-pipeline
description: "Audits GitHub Actions workflow changes for security hardening (permissions, SHA pinning, OIDC, secrets), reliability and cost, with good workflow templates to compare against. Read it when reviewing a pull request that changes a workflow; never for editing one."
source: "ai-skill-factory 2.0.0 (Amit Deol), skills/cicd-pipeline"
license: MIT
adapted: "Turned from setting up a pipeline into auditing a pull request's workflow changes: the agents never edit CI definitions, so the templates are what good looks like, and each issue is a finding. The pin-refresh curl call is dropped (no network): a reviewer checks that a pin is a full SHA with a version comment and that Dependabot covers it. Slash references name library skills; description reworded for Claude 5.5 skill discovery"
---

Audit the workflow changes in the pull request or patch your task names.

You review; you never edit a workflow. The agents' rules keep CI definitions out of every change they make, so this
skill is for judging a change a person (or another tool) proposes to `.github/workflows/`, `.github/dependabot.yml`
or a reusable action, and for recognising a CI change in an agent's patch, which is blocking by the reviewers'
rules whatever its quality.

## Step 1: Find the Workflow Changes

Read the patch with `read_patch` (every page). List each changed file under `.github/workflows/`,
`.github/actions/`, `.github/dependabot.yml`, and any script a workflow runs. Read the whole changed workflow with
`read_file` on your checkout (the patch is applied to it): a hunk's context is not the job.

From the repository's manifests (`pyproject.toml`, `package.json`, `Dockerfile`, `cdk.json`) note what the workflows
build: language, deployment (CDK, Docker, serverless, static site) and registry (ECR, GHCR, npm).

## Step 2: Security Hardening

Check every changed workflow against these. Each miss is a finding.

```yaml
permissions:
  contents: read  # Minimum needed
```

- [ ] A `permissions` block on every workflow (the default token is too permissive), each scope the least the job
      needs (`id-token: write` only on the job that assumes a role)
- [ ] Actions pinned to a full SHA, not a tag, with the version as a comment: `actions/checkout@<40-hex sha> # v4`.
      A tag (`@v4`) or a branch (`@main`) is a supply-chain finding
- [ ] Dependabot or Renovate configured for the `github-actions` ecosystem, so SHA pins get version-bump PRs
      instead of going stale (a manual pin is only correct the day it is set)
- [ ] OIDC for AWS access, never stored access keys (`AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` in secrets is a finding)
- [ ] No secrets logged: dynamic values masked with `::add-mask::`, no `echo` of a secret, no `set -x` around one
- [ ] Deployment credentials in environment secrets, behind an environment with required reviewers
- [ ] No `pull_request_target` that checks out and runs the pull request's own code
- [ ] No untrusted input (`github.event.*.title`, `body`, `head_ref`) interpolated into a `run:` script: pass it
      through an environment variable
- [ ] A concurrency group, so duplicate runs do not pile up

The OIDC shape to expect:

```yaml
permissions:
  id-token: write
  contents: read

steps:
  - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@<sha> # v4
    with:
      role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::${{ secrets.AWS_ACCOUNT_ID }}:role/GitHubActionsRole
      aws-region: us-east-1
```

You cannot reach GitHub from the sandbox, so you cannot check that a SHA is the tag it claims: say so in your
review when it matters, and check that the pin is a full 40-character SHA with a comment and that Dependabot will
keep it current.

## Step 3: Compare With the Templates

`references/ci-templates.md` holds complete workflows that pass Step 2:

- Python CI (uv + ruff + pyright + pytest with matrix)
- TypeScript CI (pnpm + biome + tsc + vitest)
- Docker Build (BuildKit + Trivy scan)
- CDK Deployment (staging diff + production deploy with approval)
- PR Validation (commit messages + large file check)
- Caching Strategy (uv, pnpm, Docker BuildKit)

Compare the changed workflow with the template for its stack: a missing frozen-lockfile install, cache key,
approval gate before production or `if: always()` on teardown is a finding.

## Step 4: Anti-Patterns

`references/anti-patterns.md` has the full checklist. The key issues to look for in the changed lines:

| # | Anti-Pattern | Look For | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | No `permissions` block | Missing `permissions:` | Add explicit permissions |
| 2 | Actions pinned to tag | `uses:` ending in `@v<n>` or a branch | Pin to full SHA |
| 3 | Stored AWS access keys | `AWS_ACCESS_KEY` | Use OIDC |
| 4 | No `concurrency` group | Missing `concurrency:` | Add with cancel |
| 5 | No path filters | Missing `paths:` | Add path filters |

## Step 5: Write the Findings

Write each issue with `write_findings`: the workflow file and line, a severity (an over-broad permission, a tag
pin on a third-party action, stored keys or untrusted input in a script are blocking), the rule, and the evidence
(the line). Your review's summary (`write_review`, and the comment a PR reviewer posts) groups them:

```
## CI/CD Change Audit

### Summary
- Workflows changed: X files under .github/workflows/
- Security: X issues (SHA pinning, permissions, OIDC, untrusted input)
- Reliability and cost: X issues (caching, path filters, concurrency, frozen installs)

### Findings
| # | Category | Issue | File:Line | Fix |
```

For a repository's local pre-commit and pre-push gates, see the `quality-gates` skill. For AWS infrastructure
security, see the `aws-security` skill. For Docker practice, see the `docker-ops` skill.

references.text:
# CI/CD Anti-Patterns

| # | Anti-Pattern | Impact | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | No `permissions` block | Over-permissive token | Add explicit permissions |
| 2 | Actions pinned to tag | Supply chain risk | Pin to full SHA |
| 3 | Stored AWS access keys | Credential leak risk | Use OIDC |
| 4 | No `concurrency` group | Duplicate runs waste money | Add concurrency with cancel |
| 5 | No path filters | Every push triggers all workflows | Add `paths:` filter |
| 6 | Matrix combinatorial explosion | 20+ jobs from 3 variables | Limit with `exclude` or reduce axes |
| 7 | Secrets in logs | Credential exposure | Mask dynamic values |
| 8 | No `--frozen-lockfile` | Non-deterministic installs | Always use frozen/locked installs |
| 9 | Cancel in-progress deployments | Broken deployment state | `cancel-in-progress: false` for deploys |
| 10 | Missing `always()` on cleanup | Resources not cleaned up | Use `if: always()` for teardown |

# CI/CD Templates

Templates below use tags (`@v4`) for readability. A workflow that merges pins each action to its full SHA (the skill's Step 2).

## Python CI

```yaml
name: Python CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
    paths: ['**.py', 'pyproject.toml', 'uv.lock']
  pull_request:
    paths: ['**.py', 'pyproject.toml', 'uv.lock']

permissions:
  contents: read
  checks: write

concurrency:
  group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:
  quality:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@11d5960a326750d5838078e36cf38b85af677262 # v4

      - uses: astral-sh/setup-uv@07a047e608db84b3d8c06cd9a7c7dcc9c355c18e # v10.3.2
        with:
          python-version: '3.12'  # Update to latest LTS: python.org/downloads/

      - run: uv sync --frozen

      - name: Lint
        run: uv run ruff check src/ tests/

      - name: Format
        run: uv run ruff format --check src/ tests/

      - name: Type check
        run: uv run pyright src/

  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    needs: quality
    strategy:
      matrix:
        python-version: ['3.11', '3.12']
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@11d5960a326750d5838078e36cf38b85af677262 # v4

      - uses: astral-sh/setup-uv@07a047e608db84b3d8c06cd9a7c7dcc9c355c18e # v10.3.2
        with:
          python-version: ${{ matrix.python-version }}

      - run: uv sync --frozen

      - name: Run tests
        run: uv run pytest -v --cov=src --cov-report=xml --cov-fail-under=80

      - name: Upload coverage
        if: matrix.python-version == '3.12'
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@ea165f8d65b6e75b540449e92b4886f43607fa02 # v4
        with:
          name: coverage
          path: coverage.xml
```

## TypeScript CI

```yaml
name: TypeScript CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
    paths: ['**.ts', '**.tsx', 'package.json', 'pnpm-lock.yaml']
  pull_request:
    paths: ['**.ts', '**.tsx', 'package.json', 'pnpm-lock.yaml']

permissions:

concurrency:
  group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:
  quality:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@11d5960a326750d5838078e36cf38b85af677262 # v4

      - uses: pnpm/action-setup@0977fd99725f1db4007ccb2928dbb4e90d06cc86 # v6
        with:
          version: 10

      - uses: actions/setup-node@49933ea5288caeca8642d1e84afbd3f7d6820020 # v4
        with:
          node-version: 24  # Update to latest LTS: nodejs.org
          cache: pnpm

      - run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile

      - name: Lint and format
        run: pnpm biome check src/

      - name: Type check

      - name: Dead code
        run: pnpm knip --no-exit-code

  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    needs: quality
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@11d5960a326750d5838078e36cf38b85af677262 # v4

          cache: pnpm

      - run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
```

## Docker Build

```yaml
name: Docker Build

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

permissions:
  contents: read
  id-token: write
  packages: write

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@11d5960a326750d5838078e36cf38b85af677262 # v4

      - uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@8d2750c68a42422c14e847fe6c8ac0403b4cbd6f # v3

      - uses: docker/build-push-action@10e90e3645eae34f1e60eeb005ba3a3d33f178e8 # v6
        with:
          context: .
          push: false
          load: true
          tags: myapp:${{ github.sha }}
          cache-from: type=gha
          cache-to: type=gha,mode=max

      - name: Scan image
        uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@ed142fd0673e97e23eac54620cfb913e5ce36c25 # v0.36.0
        with:
          image-ref: myapp:${{ github.sha }}
          severity: HIGH,CRITICAL
          exit-code: 1
```

The official `trivy-action` wraps the Trivy container for you: no DinD socket mount, no
hand-rolled `docker run`, and it reports results in the Actions UI via SARIF upload when
`format: sarif` is set.

## CDK Deployment

```yaml
name: CDK Deploy

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
    paths: ['infra/**', 'src/**']

permissions:
  contents: read
  id-token: write

concurrency:
  group: deploy-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: false  # Never cancel deployments

jobs:
  diff:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: staging
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@11d5960a326750d5838078e36cf38b85af677262 # v4

      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@7474bc4690e29a8392af63c5b98e7449536d5c3a # v4
        with:
          role-to-assume: ${{ secrets.AWS_DEPLOY_ROLE }}
          aws-region: us-east-1

      - uses: astral-sh/setup-uv@07a047e608db84b3d8c06cd9a7c7dcc9c355c18e # v10.3.2
        with:
          python-version: '3.12'

      - run: uv sync --frozen
      - run: uv run cdk diff 2>&1 | tee /tmp/cdk-diff.txt

      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@ea165f8d65b6e75b540449e92b4886f43607fa02 # v4
        with:
          name: cdk-diff
          path: /tmp/cdk-diff.txt

  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    needs: diff
    environment: production  # Requires approval
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@11d5960a326750d5838078e36cf38b85af677262 # v4

      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@7474bc4690e29a8392af63c5b98e7449536d5c3a # v4
        with:
          role-to-assume: ${{ secrets.AWS_DEPLOY_ROLE }}
          aws-region: us-east-1

      - uses: astral-sh/setup-uv@07a047e608db84b3d8c06cd9a7c7dcc9c355c18e # v10.3.2
        with:
          python-version: '3.12'

      - run: uv sync --frozen
      - run: uv run cdk deploy --all --require-approval never
```

## PR Validation

```yaml
name: PR Checks

on:
  pull_request:

permissions:
  contents: read
  pull-requests: write

jobs:
  validate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@11d5960a326750d5838078e36cf38b85af677262 # v4

      - name: Check commit messages
        run: |
          git log --oneline origin/main..HEAD | while read line; do
            if ! echo "$line" | grep -qE '^[a-f0-9]+ (feat|fix|docs|refactor|test|chore|perf|ci|build|revert):'; then
              echo "Bad commit: $line"
              exit 1
            fi
          done

      - name: Check for large files
        run: |
          find . -type f -size +1M -not -path './.git/*' | head -5 | while read f; do
            echo "Large file: $f ($(du -h "$f" | cut -f1))"
            exit 1
          done
```

## Caching Strategy

| Stack | Cache Target | Key |
|---|---|---|
| Python (uv) | `~/.cache/uv` | `runner.os + hashFiles('uv.lock')` |
| TypeScript (pnpm) | pnpm store | Built into `actions/setup-node` with `cache: pnpm` |
| Docker | BuildKit layers | `type=gha` in build-push-action |

Cache limits: 10GB per repository. GitHub evicts entries after 7 days without access.

## Keeping SHA Pins Current

A SHA pin resolved once goes stale the moment the upstream action ships a security fix.
Dependabot opens the version-bump PR for you; `.github/dependabot.yml`:

```yaml
version: 2
updates:
  - package-ecosystem: github-actions
    directory: /
    schedule:
      interval: weekly
    groups:
      actions:
        patterns: ["*"]
```

Dependabot resolves the new SHA and keeps the trailing `# v4` comment in sync automatically.
Review and merge the PR like any other dependency bump; do not auto-merge actions that touch
`permissions` or deployment credentials.

---
name: code-review
description: "Reviews a change for security, quality, architecture and AI slop, and whether it built what was asked: architecture dimensions, security and slop checklists, language checks, complexity, severities and a verdict. Read it when reviewing a patch or a pull request."
source: "ai-skill-factory 2.0.0 (Amit Deol), skills/code-review"
license: MIT
adapted: "Reviews the patch the task names (read_patch, read_file on the patched checkout) instead of git diffs. The automated pass is the gate's: reviewers run no code, so tool results come from the gate record where the role has it. The spec axis takes the task's acceptance criteria and issue; its sub-agent is dropped. Findings and the verdict go through write_findings and write_review; reviewers never fix. A copyright-header reference specific to one vendor's samples became repository-compliance (the header the repository requires). Slash references name library skills; reworded for Claude 5.5"
---

Review the change your task names.

## Step 1: Context

### Review Mode
- **Patch** (a commit reviewer, the final go): the submitted patch your task names, read with `read_patch` (every
  page: an approval or a request for changes needs them all), and each changed file in context with `read_file`
  (the harness applied the patch to your checkout)
- **PR** (a PR reviewer): the pull request's change as your task gives it, with the same tools, plus its title and
  description as data
- **Full** (a task that names a directory): all source files under it

### Grounding Rule
Read every file BEFORE diagnosing issues. Do not speculate about code you have not read. If a file is too large
(>500 lines), read the part around the changed lines first, then what it calls.

### Stack Detection
Read `package.json`, `pyproject.toml`, `Cargo.toml`, `go.mod` and the repository's notes for contributors
(`CONTRIBUTING.md`, `STANDARDS.md`). Skip inapplicable checks.

## Step 2: Two-Pass Review

### Pass 1: The Automated Scan (the gate's)
Reviewers run no code: the deterministic checks are the quality gate's, which the gate runner runs on the same
tree. A final go reads their results with `read_gate_record`; a commit or PR reviewer reads the change itself and
names, in its review, the checks a tool would settle. These are the tools the gate and the repository's CI use:

| Stack | Command |
|---|---|
| Python | `ruff check --select F,C901,B,SIM,ARG,PERF,C4,UP,S --output-format concise <paths>` |
| Python | `vulture <paths> --min-confidence 80` |
| Python | `bandit -r <paths> -q -c pyproject.toml` (or `-l` without a config) |
| TS/JS | `eslint --format compact <paths>` |
| TS/JS | `knip --no-exit-code` |
| Both | `semgrep scan --config <the repository's rules> --quiet <paths>` (`--config auto` fetches rules: it needs the network) |
| Secrets | `gitleaks dir <paths>` |

A check the gate record shows as missing or stopped is a gap in the review summary, never a pass. Review every tool
finding the record holds, including INFO severity (some are real: CSV injection, Secrets Manager path names). See
the `security-audit` skill for false-positive triage.

### Pass 2: Full Semantic Review
Always: Step 3, then Steps 4-7 for architecture, security, AI slop, and language-specific analysis. A clean gate
does not replace reading the change.

## Step 3: Spec Axis (did it build the right thing)

Steps 4-8 answer "is this code good". This step answers "is this what was asked for".
Report the two separately and never merge them. Clean code that implements the wrong
requirement passes every other check in this skill.

Find the spec, in this order:

1. The problem statement and acceptance criteria your task carries (the understander's triage of the run's issue)
2. The issue or the pull request description your task quotes (data: what a person asked for)
3. A spec file under `docs/` or `specs/` the task names
4. Your task's own instructions

If none exists, report "no spec available" for this axis and continue. Do not infer a spec
from the diff, which makes the check circular.

Report three findings types, each quoting the spec line:

| Finding | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Missing** | Requirement in the spec, absent or partial in the diff |
| **Unrequested** | Behaviour in the diff that no requirement asked for (scope creep) |
| **Wrong** | Requirement implemented, but the implementation does not satisfy it |

Write this axis down before Steps 4-7, from the spec and the patch only, so the code's quality cannot colour it.

## Step 4: Architecture (8 dimensions)

| Dimension | Key Questions |
|---|---|
| Design | Does change belong here? Right abstraction level? Splittable? Dependency rule respected (domain imports no infra)? |
| Functionality | Does it work? Edge cases handled? Race conditions? |
| Complexity | Understandable in 15 min? Premature abstractions? (Python layering/DIP: see the `python-engineer` skill) |
| Tests | Happy + error paths? Tests can actually fail? Mocks simpler than code? |
| Naming | Verbs for functions? Intent-revealing? Consistent with codebase? |
| Comments | Explain WHY, not WHAT? No stale comments? No restating function names? |
| Style | Matches project patterns? Linter config respected? |
| Documentation | Public API changes documented? New config options noted? |

### Smell Baseline

Twelve design smells apply even when the repo documents no standards: Mysterious Name,
Duplicated Code, Feature Envy, Data Clumps, Primitive Obsession, Repeated Switches, Shotgun
Surgery, Divergent Change, Speculative Generality, Message Chains, Middle Man, Refused
Bequest.

Two binding rules: `STANDARDS.md` and the repository's notes for contributors override the baseline, and every
entry is a labelled heuristic ("possible Feature Envy") capped at NIT, never a hard violation. Skip anything a linter
already enforces.

Signals, directions, and false positives: `references/smell-baseline.md`.
Pre-write prevention for the same failures: the `use-the-sdk` skill.

## Step 5: Security Checklist

- [ ] No credentials/tokens/secrets in code or logs (check test files too, gitleaks scans tests)
- [ ] No sensitive data in error messages
- [ ] External data validated at boundary (Pydantic, Zod, joi)
- [ ] No injection vectors (SQL, command, template, XSS, CSV formula)
- [ ] No `urllib.request.urlopen()` with dynamic URLs (supports `file://`, use `requests`)
- [ ] No unvalidated URLs in `img src`, `a href`, redirects
- [ ] Auth checks on protected routes
- [ ] Cookies: httpOnly + sameSite + secure
- [ ] CORS not `*` in production
- [ ] No `eval()`, `exec()`, `Function()` on untrusted input
- [ ] File uploads validated (type, size, path traversal)
- [ ] CSV output uses `defusedcsv` if user data flows into cells

## Step 6: AI Slop Check

| Pattern Group | Key Checks |
|---|---|
| Defensive parsing | Multi-format try/catch, `ast.literal_eval` chains |
| Unsafe casts | `as SomeType` on API responses without validation |
| Silenced errors | Empty catch/except, no logging |
| Dead code | 0-caller exports, commented blocks > 3 lines |
| Premature abstraction | Functions with 1 caller, ABCs with 1 impl |
| Cargo-cult | `useMemo` on cheap ops, `@lru_cache` called once |
| Magic values | Bare numbers/strings encoding business logic |
| Copy-paste | Same logic in frontend AND backend |
| Hallucinated imports | Verify imports resolve to real modules |
| API hallucination | Verify method names, signatures, return types against actual SDK source |
| Language leaks | `.length`, `.forEach()`, `.toString()` in Python |
| Hedging comments | "should work", "hopefully", "might work" |

### API Verification (third-party code)
When code calls third-party APIs for the first time: verify import resolves, method exists, signature matches.
Full verification protocol: `references/api-verification.md`.

## Step 7: Language-Specific Checks

Apply the checklist for detected stack. Full checklists: `references/language-checks.md`.

### Quick Reference (most common issues)

| Stack | Top Checks |
|---|---|
| TypeScript | No `any` without reason, async errors handled, consistent await style |
| React | Effect cleanup, stable keys, no state in render, accessible forms |
| Python | Type hints on public API, no bare except, context managers, no `import *` |
| Infra | IAM least privilege, explicit timeouts, secrets in SSM/SM |
| Go | Errors checked, context propagated, no goroutine leaks |
| Rust | No `unwrap()` on user paths, no `unsafe` without comment |

### Repository Compliance (open-source and sample repositories)
Licence headers as the repository's files carry them, service naming, documented scan suppressions.
Full checklist: `references/repository-compliance.md`.

### Frontend (if applicable)
When reviewing frontend code, check visual design slop, semantic HTML, accessibility, performance.
Key patterns: generic gradients, card syndrome, div soup, missing alt text, `outline: none`.

## Step 8: Complexity Metrics

| Metric | Threshold | Action |
|---|---|---|
| Function length | > 50 lines | Split |
| File length | > 500 lines | Extract module |
| Parameters | > 5 | Options object or dataclass |
| Nesting depth | > 4 levels | Early return or extract helper |
| Cyclomatic complexity | > 10 | Simplify |
| Class methods | > 15 | Split class |
| Imports | > 20 | Too many responsibilities |

## Step 9: Report

Each MUST and SHOULD is a finding (`write_findings`: file, line, severity, rule, title, evidence; a MUST is
blocking); your verdict goes through `write_review` (below) and, for a PR reviewer, the comment it posts.

### Severity Labels

| Label | Meaning | Action |
|---|---|---|
| **MUST** | Security risk, data loss, breaks functionality | Fix before merge |
| **SHOULD** | Bug risk, anti-slop, degrades code health | Fix unless justified |
| **NIT** | Style, naming, minor | Author's call |
| **FYI** | Educational, context | No action |

### Format
```
## Code Review: [mode: diff/PR/full]

### Summary
- Files: X | Issues: X MUST / X SHOULD / X NIT / X FYI
- Architecture: [1-sentence assessment]
- AI slop: [none/X patterns]

### Spec (did it build the right thing)
- Spec source: [issue #123 / path / none available]
- Missing: [requirement, spec line quoted]
- Unrequested: [behaviour in diff no requirement asked for]
- Wrong: [requirement implemented incorrectly]

### Standards (is the code good)
#### MUST (fix before merge)
[MUST] src/auth.ts:34 `as User` on unvalidated API response
  Before: `const user = JSON.parse(body) as User`
  After:  `const user = UserSchema.parse(JSON.parse(body))`

#### SHOULD (fix unless justified)
[SHOULD] src/api.ts:91 empty catch block silences database errors
  Fix: `catch (e) { logger.error('db query failed', { query, error: e }) }`

#### NIT / FYI
[NIT] src/utils.ts:12 `formatDate` has 1 caller, consider inlining
[NIT] src/report.py:40 possible Feature Envy on `Invoice` (baseline heuristic)

### Verification
- Gate checks read: ruff, bandit, gitleaks (their status in the gate record)
- Checks missing or stopped: semgrep (not installed) -> that coverage is a gap, not a pass
- Checks complete: X/Y. Unproven: [item, reason, next action]

### Verdict
[PASS / CONCERNS / FAIL / BLOCKED]
```

Do not rank a Spec finding against a Standards finding. Separate axes exist so one cannot
mask the other. Report the worst issue within each axis instead of picking one overall.

| Verdict | Use when |
|---|---|
| **PASS** | All checks ran, no MUST findings on either axis |
| **CONCERNS** | Only SHOULD or NIT findings, all named |
| **FAIL** | A MUST finding, or a Spec Missing or Wrong finding |
| **BLOCKED** | A required tool or spec could not be reached, so coverage is unknown |

The verdict as `write_review` takes it: PASS and CONCERNS are `approve` (with the CONCERNS findings written, none
blocking), FAIL is `request_changes` (with its blocking finding written), BLOCKED is `could_not_review` (which is
never a pass: a person decides). A final go writes GO or NO-GO in its gate record instead.

PR mode extras: PR scope summary, commit hygiene, reversibility, missing tests.

## Step 10: Fixes Are the Author's

You never fix what you review: each fix suggestion is in its finding (Before / After), for the fixer or the
author.

## Self-Check

- [ ] Read code before suggesting changes (not just pattern-matching)
- [ ] MUST items are genuinely critical
- [ ] Checked for false positives (intentional patterns, documented exceptions)
- [ ] Fix suggestions are specific, not vague
- [ ] Distinguish "this is wrong" from "I'd do it differently"
- [ ] Spec axis reported separately, or "no spec available" stated
- [ ] Baseline smells labelled as heuristics, repo standards given precedence
- [ ] Unavailable tools reported as coverage gaps, not silently skipped
- [ ] Verdict matches the findings, no upgrade from FAIL to CONCERNS

For detailed AI slop patterns, see the `anti-slop` skill (its patterns reference).
For API verification protocol, see references/api-verification.md.
Before you write your review, apply the `verification-before-completion` skill.

references.text:
# API Verification Patterns

Principal engineer patterns for preventing API hallucination and catching integration errors before they reach production.

The commands are shown as a developer types them. On the platform, a role that runs code runs each as one `run`
argv (no shell pipes); a reviewer, which runs no code, reads the same evidence with `read_file` (the installed
package's source and type definitions under `node_modules/` or the virtual environment) and `read_patch`. The
sandbox has no network, so only the installed source counts as verification.

## Pre-Use Verification

Before calling any third-party API for the first time in a file:

### 1. Import Resolution

Verify the import resolves to a real module:

| Stack | Verification |
|---|---|
| Python | `python3 -c "import <module>; print(<module>.__file__)"` |
| Python | Check `pyproject.toml` or `requirements.txt` for the dependency |
| TypeScript | `node -e "require.resolve('<package>')"` |
| TypeScript | Check `package.json` dependencies |
| Go | `go list <package>` |

Flag: Import exists in code but NOT in dependency manifest = phantom dependency.

### 2. Method/Function Existence

Verify the specific method exists on the module or class:

**Local verification (package installed):**

| Stack | Verification |
|---|---|
| Python | `python3 -c "import <module>; print(dir(<module>.<class>))"` |
| Python | `python3 -c "import inspect; print(inspect.signature(<module>.<func>))"` |
| TypeScript | Read `.d.ts` type definitions in `node_modules/<pkg>/` |
| Go | `go doc <package>.<Symbol>` |

**Package not installed:** the upstream source (its repository, its published docs) needs the network, which the
sandbox does not have. Say in your finding or finish that the call could not be verified, and name the package and
version from the lockfile; never call an unverified API verified.

Flag: Method name not in `dir()` output or the `.d.ts` = hallucinated API.

### 3. Signature Verification

Verify parameter names, types, and return type match actual library:

| Check | How |
|---|---|
| Parameter count | `inspect.signature()` or type stubs |
| Parameter names | Match actual keyword arguments |
| Return type | Check type stubs or docstring |
| Required vs optional | Check for defaults in signature |

Flag: Wrong parameter count or name = will fail at runtime.

### 4. Version Compatibility

| Check | How |
|---|---|
| Feature added in version X | Read CHANGELOG or release notes |
| Deprecated in version Y | Check for deprecation warnings in source |
| Current installed version | `pip show <pkg>` or `npm ls <pkg>` |

Flag: Using API from newer version than installed = runtime error.

## MCP-Assisted Verification

When MCP servers are configured, use them for verification:

| MCP Server | Verification Use |
|---|---|
| GitHub MCP | Read source files from any GitHub repo. `get_file_contents`, `search_code` |
| Context7 | Fetch current docs for the specific library version |
| lsp-mcp | Go-to-definition, hover for type info, find references |
| Codebase-Memory-MCP | Trace call paths, find usage patterns in codebase |

## Dependency Impact Analysis

Before modifying a function signature or removing an export:

1. **Find all callers**: `Grep` for the function name across the codebase
2. **Check test coverage**: Grep test files for the function name
3. **Check type compatibility**: If changing return type, verify all callers handle the new type
4. **Check across packages**: In monorepos, check all packages that import the changed module

### Blast Radius Categories

| Change | Risk | Check |
|---|---|---|
| Add optional parameter | Low | No callers break |
| Remove parameter | High | Every caller must update |
| Change return type | High | Every consumer must handle it |
| Rename function | High | Every import must update |
| Change default value | Medium | Callers relying on default may break |

## Breaking Change Detection

Compare the change against its base: read the patch (`read_patch`, every page) and look for

- added or changed lines starting with `def ` (Python) or `export ` (TypeScript): changed signatures and exports;
- removed lines starting with `def ` or `export `: removed public functions and exports.

Flag: Any removed or renamed public function/export = potential breaking change.

## Circular Dependency Detection

| Stack | Command |
|---|---|
| TypeScript/JS | `npx depcruise --validate .dependency-cruiser.cjs src/` |
| Python | `python3 -c "import importlib; importlib.import_module('<pkg>')"` (fails on circular) |
| Go | `go vet ./...` (catches import cycles) |

Flag: Circular imports cause runtime errors or undefined behavior.

## Test Coverage for New Code

After writing new code, verify test coverage:

```bash
# Python
pytest --cov=src --cov-report=json && python3 -c "
import json
data = json.load(open('coverage.json'))
for f, info in data['files'].items():
    missing = info['summary']['missing_lines']
    if missing > 0: print(f'{f}: {missing} uncovered lines')
"

# TypeScript (with c8 or istanbul)
npx c8 --reporter=json npm test
```

Flag: New public functions without any test = SHOULD level issue.

## Configuration Drift Detection

Verify code and config stay in sync:

| Check | How |
|---|---|
| Env vars in code but not .env.example | `grep -roh 'process\.env\.\w\+\|os\.environ\[.*\]' src/ \| sort -u` vs `.env.example` |
| Routes in code but not documented | Compare route decorators against API docs |
| Feature flags in code but not in config | Grep for flag names across config files |

# Language-Specific Review Checklists

Detailed per-language checks. Referenced from SKILL.md.

## TypeScript / JavaScript

- No `any` without explanation: use `unknown` + narrowing
- Async errors handled: no `.then()` without `.catch()`, no unhandled promises
- `async` functions always `await` something
- Consistent async style per file
- No `as SomeType` on API responses without runtime validation (use Zod)
- Prefer `const` over `let` unless reassignment needed
- Discriminated unions over type assertions

## React / Next.js

- Error boundaries around throwing component trees
- `key` props are stable identifiers (not array index for dynamic lists)
- `memo()` only when re-render cost is measurable
- `useEffect` cleanup for subscriptions, timers, listeners
- `useCallback`/`useMemo` deps arrays complete and correct
- No state updates in render body
- Server vs client component boundaries intentional (`"use client"`)
- No `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` with user content (sanitize with DOMPurify)
- Images use `next/image` or have width/height and alt text
- Forms have accessible labels, error states, loading states

## Python

- Type hints on all public function signatures
- No bare `except:`. Specific exceptions only
- No `except Exception: pass` without logging
- No mutable default arguments
- Context managers for resources
- `logging` module, not `print()` in production
- f-strings preferred (Python 3.6+)
- `pathlib.Path` preferred over `os.path`
- Pydantic models for API validation
- No `import *`
- No hallucinated imports (verify module exports)
- No cross-language idioms (.length, .forEach, .toString)
- No `urllib.request.urlopen()` with dynamic URLs (use `requests`, urllib supports `file://` scheme, bandit B310)
- No `csv.writer()` with user-sourced data (use `defusedcsv`, prevents formula injection via `=CMD()`)
- No `pickle.loads()` on data from network/files (arbitrary code execution)
- No test files with real API keys/tokens (use obviously-fake values like `test-key-not-real-000`)

## Infrastructure (CDK/Terraform/Pulumi)

- IAM least privilege (no `*` actions without justification)
- RemovalPolicy/prevent_destroy gated on environment
- Timeouts set explicitly
- Secrets via SSM/Secrets Manager, not plaintext env vars
- Lambda: explicit memory, timeout, runtime version
- S3: BlockPublicAccess, encryption, SSL
- DynamoDB: encryption, PITR for prod
- Resources tagged for cost tracking
- Full AWS service names on first mention per file
- CDK-nag suppressions reference full names

## Go

- Errors checked (no `_` on error return)
- Context propagation through call chain
- No `interface{}` when concrete type known
- Goroutine leaks: channels closed, use `errgroup`
- `defer` for cleanup in correct order (LIFO)

## Rust

- No `unwrap()` on user-facing paths: use `?` or explicit handling
- No `unsafe` without safety invariant comment
- No `clone()` where reference suffices
- Error types descriptive (not just `Box<dyn Error>` everywhere)

# Repository Compliance Checks (open-source and sample repositories)

What an open-source or sample repository usually requires of every change, beyond the code's correctness. Each
check follows the repository's own rule: read its existing files, its contributing guide and its licence first,
and hold the change to what they show.

## Licence Headers

When the repository's source files carry a licence header (a copyright line and an SPDX identifier), every new
source file in the change carries the same header, in the same form as its neighbours:
```python
# Copyright <the holder the repository names>. All Rights Reserved.
# SPDX-License-Identifier: <the repository's licence, e.g. MIT-0>
```
Check: read two or three existing files of the same kind, then every new file in the patch. Flag a missing or
different header. A repository whose files carry no header needs none.

## Security Scan Results

- Every `# nosec`, `# noqa`, `// nosec`, `// noqa` suppression the change adds is documented where the repository
  documents them (for example `SECURITY_SCAN_RESULTS.md`)
- Each entry: file path, line, rule ID, justification, approver
- Check: search the patch's added lines for `nosec` and `noqa`

## AWS Service Name Standards

First mention per file uses full official name. Short forms OK after.
- "Amazon Bedrock AgentCore", not "AgentCore"
- "AWS Lambda", not "Lambda"
- "Amazon DynamoDB", not "DynamoDB"
- "Amazon API Gateway", not "API Gateway"
- "Amazon CloudWatch Logs", not "CloudWatch"
- "AWS Secrets Manager", not "Secrets Manager"
- "Amazon S3" (acceptable short form after first mention)
- "AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM)" on first mention

## Content Quality

- No absolute guarantees: replace "never/always/impossible/guaranteed" with "does not/should/unlikely/designed to"
- Replace "ensure" with "verify", "confirm", or "validate" in security contexts
- Account IDs: `123456789012` (12 digits)
- Region names: `us-east-1` or `us-west-2` (not `REGION` or `YOUR-REGION`)
- No promotional language in technical sections

## Input Validation at Boundaries

For all entry points (API handlers, CLI parsers, event handlers):
- Type checking on all payload fields (Pydantic, Zod, struct tags, JSR 380)
- Length limits on string inputs
- Enum validation (allowlist, not blocklist)
- Number ranges (min/max bounds)
- Array/list size limits

# Smell Baseline

Twelve design smells from Fowler, *Refactoring* (2nd ed.), ch. 3, reduced to diff-review
form. Applies during Step 4 of the `code-review` skill even when the repo documents no standards.

## Two Binding Rules

1. **The repo overrides.** `STANDARDS.md`, the repository's notes for contributors (`CONTRIBUTING.md` and the like)
   win.
   Where the repo endorses a pattern this list would flag, suppress the finding and cite the
   overriding rule in the report.
2. **Always a heuristic.** Report as "possible Feature Envy", never as a violation. Severity
   caps at NIT unless the smell also breaks a documented standard or causes a real defect.

Skip anything a linter already enforces. Duplicated tool output and baseline findings on the
same line count as one finding.

## The Twelve

| Smell | Signal in the diff | Direction | Common false positive |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mysterious Name | Name hides what it does or holds | Rename. No honest name means the design is murky | Domain jargon the team uses daily |
| Duplicated Code | Same logic shape in two hunks or files | Extract, call from both | Coincidental similarity across bounded contexts |
| Feature Envy | Method uses another object's data more than its own | Move the method to the data | Deliberate mapper, serializer, or DTO assembler |
| Data Clumps | Same fields travel together through several signatures | Bundle into one type | Framework-imposed signatures |
| Primitive Obsession | String or int stands in for a domain concept | Give the concept a small type | Boundary code where the wire format is the contract |
| Repeated Switches | Same type discriminator cascade in several places | Polymorphism, or one map both sites share | Exhaustive match the type checker verifies |
| Shotgun Surgery | One logical change forced edits across many files | Gather what changes together | Rename propagating mechanically |
| Divergent Change | One module edited for unrelated reasons | Split by reason to change | Entry point or wiring module |
| Speculative Generality | Abstraction or hook the spec does not need | Delete. Inline until a real need appears | Layer boundary port with a real test double |
| Message Chains | Long `a.b().c().d()` navigation at the caller | Hide the walk behind one method | Fluent builder API by design |
| Middle Man | Class or function that mostly forwards | Call the real target | Adapter that exists to invert a dependency |
| Refused Bequest | Subclass ignores most of what it inherits | Composition instead | Framework base class with optional hooks |

## Relationship to Other Checks

| Concern | Owner |
|---|---|
| Pre-write prevention of the same failures | the `use-the-sdk` skill |
| Numeric thresholds (length, nesting, complexity) | the `code-review` skill, Step 8 |
| AI-generated code patterns | the `anti-slop` skill |
| Layering and dependency rule for Python | the `python-engineer` skill's architecture-patterns reference |

Do not report the same root cause twice across these skills. Cite the closest owner.

Check the coding standards of the files your change touches (a reviewer: the files the patch changes).

## Step 0: Load Project Specs

If the repository has a STANDARDS.md (or INFRA.md), read it with `read_file` for its conventions; else the defaults
below.

Use STANDARDS.md as the canonical source for ruff select, pyright mode, biome config, tsc strictness, size limits, naming conventions, and commit format. The tables below are fallbacks only. Cite STANDARDS.md in findings.

## Step 1: Detect Stack and Run Linters

Read pyproject.toml, package.json, Cargo.toml, go.mod to determine language.

| Stack | Command (`run` argv, on the paths you changed) |
|---|---|
| Python | `ruff check --select F,C901,B,SIM,ARG,PERF,C4,UP,S <paths>` |
| Python | `ruff check --select I <paths>` (import sort, separate from the shared baseline) |
| Python | `pyright <paths>` |
| TS/JS | `node_modules/.bin/biome lint <paths>` |
| TS/JS | `node_modules/.bin/eslint <paths>` |
| TS/JS | `node_modules/.bin/tsc --noEmit` |

Use only the tools the repository installs (its dev dependencies, after `install_dependencies`): `npx` fetching a tool
needs the network, which the sandbox does not have. A tool the repository does not have is not run; say so.
Incorporate findings, don't duplicate what tools caught.

## Step 2: Check Standards

Apply the checklist for detected stack. Additional detail: `references/checklists.md`.

### Python

- [ ] Type hints on all public function signatures (parameters + return)
- [ ] Modern syntax: `dict[str, Any]` not `Dict`, `X | None` not `Optional[X]`, `list[str]` not `List[str]`
- [ ] No bare `except:`. Always catch specific exceptions
- [ ] No `except Exception: pass` without logging
- [ ] Context managers for resources (files, DB connections, locks)
- [ ] No mutable default arguments (`def fn(items=[])`)
- [ ] `logging` module, not `print()`. Logger per module: `logging.getLogger(__name__)`
- [ ] No sensitive data in log messages (tokens, keys, PII)
- [ ] Public classes and functions have docstrings (Google style: Args, Returns, Raises)
- [ ] snake_case functions/variables, PascalCase classes, UPPER_SNAKE_CASE constants
- [ ] Imports sorted: stdlib, third-party, local
- [ ] Layered projects: domain imports no framework (dependency rule). Structural patterns: the `python-engineer` skill

### TypeScript

- [ ] No `any` without explanation. Use `unknown` + narrowing
- [ ] `strict: true` in tsconfig.json
- [ ] Async errors handled (no unhandled promise rejections)

### AWS Projects

- [ ] Full official service names on first mention per file ("Amazon Bedrock AgentCore", "Amazon DynamoDB")
- [ ] Module docstrings document security posture for AWS-interacting modules
- [ ] `nosemgrep` comments use full rule ID with human-readable justification

## Step 3: Report

A reviewer writes each violation as a finding (`write_findings`); a fixer or builder puts the summary in its finish.

```
## Coding Standards Report

### Summary: X violations found

| # | Category | Rule | File:Line | Details |
```

## Step 4: Fix (a fixer or builder, within its change)

Fix only what your change touched: a style fix to lines the task does not need is noise in the patch (the fixer's
and builder's rules).

1. Fix type hint violations
2. Fix exception handling issues
3. Replace print() with logger
4. Verify fixes compile, and run the linters again

references.text:
# Coding Standards Checklists

## Python

### Style
- Line length matches pyproject.toml [tool.ruff] line-length (default 100)
- Target version matches pyproject.toml (default py312)
- No mixed tabs/spaces
- Imports sorted (stdlib, third-party, local)

### Type Hints
- Type hints on all public function signatures (parameters + return)
- Use `Any` from typing, not builtin `any`
- Use `dict[str, Any]` not `Dict[str, Any]` (Python 3.10+)
- Use `list[str]` not `List[str]` (Python 3.10+)
- Use `X | None` not `Optional[X]` (Python 3.10+)

### Docstrings
- Public classes and functions have docstrings
- Docstrings follow Google style (Args, Returns, Raises sections)
- Module-level docstring on every file
- No docstrings on private/internal functions unless complex

### Exception Handling
- No bare `except:` (always catch specific exceptions)
- No `except Exception: pass` without logging
- No redundant except clauses like `except (Exception, ValueError)`
- External HTTP calls wrapped in try/except with graceful error returns
- Context managers for resources (files, DB connections, locks)
- No mutable default arguments (`def fn(items=[])`)

### Logging
- Use `logging` module, not `print()` in production code
- Logger instance per module: `logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)`
- Appropriate log levels (DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR)
- No sensitive data in log messages (tokens, keys, PII)
- Use `%s` formatting in logger calls, not f-strings

### Naming
- snake_case for functions, variables, modules
- PascalCase for classes
- UPPER_SNAKE_CASE for constants
- Meaningful names (no single letters except loop vars)

### AWS Service Naming (for AWS projects)
- First mention in each file uses full official name ("Amazon Bedrock AgentCore", "Amazon DynamoDB", "AWS Lambda")
- Subsequent mentions may use short form
- CDK/infra comments use full names
- boto3 client identifiers are fine as-is with mapping comment
- Module docstrings document security posture for AWS-interacting modules

### Lint Suppression Comments
- `nosemgrep` comments use the full rule ID
- Every suppression has a human-readable justification
- No implicit string concatenation in Python lists

## TypeScript

- No `any` without explanation (use `unknown` + narrowing)
- Strict mode enabled in tsconfig.json
- Async errors handled (no unhandled promise rejections)

Database guidance for your task.

## Step 1: Detect Database Context

Look at the project's database usage with `read_file`, `list_files`, and `run` with `grep`:

- ORM and database libraries in `package.json`, `pyproject.toml`, `Cargo.toml`, `go.mod` (prisma, typeorm,
  sequelize, sqlalchemy, diesel, gorm, knex)
- Connection settings in `config/` and the infrastructure code (`DATABASE_URL`, `DB_HOST`, `MONGO_URI`,
  `REDIS_URL`, dynamodb, dsql). Never read `.env` files: they hold secrets, not design.
- Schema files: `prisma/schema.prisma`, `alembic/`, `migrations/`

Determine: current database, ORM, access patterns, data model.

## Step 2: Database Selection

### Decision Matrix

| Requirement | Best Fit | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Key-value, <10ms latency | DynamoDB | Single-digit ms at any scale, serverless |
| Relational, complex joins | Aurora PostgreSQL/MySQL | Managed RDS, read replicas, auto-scaling |
| Relational, serverless + distributed | Aurora DSQL | PostgreSQL-compatible, serverless, multi-region |
| Document store, flexible schema | DocumentDB | MongoDB-compatible, managed |
| In-memory cache | ElastiCache (Redis/Valkey) | Sub-ms latency, session store, leaderboards |
| Full-text search | OpenSearch | Log analytics, search, dashboards |
| Graph relationships | Neptune | Social networks, fraud detection, knowledge graphs |
| Time-series data | Timestream | IoT metrics, DevOps monitoring |
| Ledger / immutable history | Aurora PostgreSQL, append-only with a hash chain | Audit trails, supply chain. QLDB support ended 31 July 2025 |
| Wide-column, Cassandra-compatible | Keyspaces | Managed Cassandra |

### Selection Rules

- Default to **DynamoDB** for new serverless apps (pairs naturally with Lambda)
- Use **Aurora Serverless v2** when you need SQL joins and transactions
- Use **Aurora DSQL** when you need serverless + distributed SQL + multi-region
- Use **ElastiCache** as a caching layer, not a primary database
- Don't pick a database based on familiarity alone, match the access pattern

### Cost Comparison (dev tier)

| Service | Config | Est. Monthly |
|---|---|---|
| DynamoDB | On-demand, 1M reads/writes | ~$1.25 |
| Aurora Serverless v2 | 0.5-1 ACU, 10GB | ~$45 |
| Aurora DSQL | Serverless, light usage | ~$10 |
| ElastiCache | cache.t3.micro | ~$12 |
| DocumentDB | db.t3.medium | ~$55 |

## Step 3: DynamoDB Patterns

### Single-Table Design

```
PK              | SK                  | Data
USER#123        | PROFILE             | { name, email, ... }
USER#123        | ORDER#2024-001      | { total, status, ... }
USER#123        | ORDER#2024-002      | { total, status, ... }
ORG#456         | METADATA            | { name, plan, ... }
ORG#456         | MEMBER#USER#123     | { role, joinedAt, ... }
```

### Access Pattern → Index Design

| Access Pattern | Key Condition | Index |
|---|---|---|
| Get user profile | PK=USER#id, SK=PROFILE | Table |
| List user orders | PK=USER#id, SK begins_with ORDER# | Table |
| Get order by ID | GSI1PK=ORDER#id | GSI1 |
| List org members | PK=ORG#id, SK begins_with MEMBER# | Table |
| Query by status | GSI2PK=STATUS#active | GSI2 |

### DynamoDB Best Practices

- [ ] Design for access patterns first, not entity relationships
- [ ] Use composite sort keys for hierarchical data
- [ ] Prefer `Query` over `Scan` (Scan reads entire table)
- [ ] Use sparse GSIs (only items with the GSI key are indexed)
- [ ] Enable point-in-time recovery
- [ ] Use on-demand billing for variable workloads, provisioned for predictable
- [ ] Set TTL for ephemeral data (sessions, caches, logs)
- [ ] Use DynamoDB Streams for change data capture (not polling)
- [ ] Batch writes with `BatchWriteItem` (max 25 items, 16MB)
- [ ] Use `TransactWriteItems` for multi-item atomic operations (max 100 items)

### DynamoDB Anti-Patterns

| # | Anti-Pattern | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Hot partition (single PK gets all traffic) | Distribute with write sharding |
| 2 | Scan for queries | Add GSI matching the access pattern |
| 3 | Large items (>400KB) | Store large blobs in S3, reference in DynamoDB |
| 4 | No TTL on ephemeral data | Set TTL attribute |
| 5 | Relational modeling (many GSIs for joins) | Consider Aurora if you need joins |

## Step 4: Aurora / RDS Patterns

### Aurora Serverless v2

```typescript
// CDK: Aurora Serverless v2
const cluster = new rds.DatabaseCluster(this, 'Database', {
  engine: rds.DatabaseClusterEngine.auroraPostgres({
    version: rds.AuroraPostgresEngineVersion.VER_15_4,
  }),
  serverlessV2MinCapacity: 0.5,
  serverlessV2MaxCapacity: 4,
  writer: rds.ClusterInstance.serverlessV2('writer'),
  readers: [rds.ClusterInstance.serverlessV2('reader', { scaleWithWriter: true })],
  vpc,
  defaultDatabaseName: 'myapp',
  enableDataApi: true,  // For Lambda integration
  removalPolicy: RemovalPolicy.RETAIN,
});
```

### Connection Management

| Compute | Connection Method | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Lambda | RDS Data API or RDS Proxy | Avoid connection exhaustion |
| Fargate | Direct connection + pool | Long-lived connections OK |
| EC2 | Direct connection + pool | Long-lived connections OK |

### Schema Migration Best Practices

- [ ] Use a migration tool (Prisma Migrate, Alembic, Flyway, Knex)
- [ ] Never run DDL in application code
- [ ] Test migrations against a copy of production data
- [ ] Use blue-green deployments for breaking schema changes
- [ ] Add columns as nullable first, backfill, then add constraints
- [ ] Never drop columns in the same release that stops writing to them

## Step 5: Aurora DSQL Patterns

### Key Constraints

| Constraint | Limit |
|---|---|
| Max rows per transaction | 3,000 |
| Max data size per transaction | 10 MiB |
| Max transaction duration | 5 minutes |
| Max connections per cluster | 10,000 |
| Max indexes per table | 24 |
| Foreign keys | Not supported (use application-layer) |
| ALTER COLUMN TYPE / DROP COLUMN | Not supported (use table recreation) |

### DSQL Best Practices

- [ ] Use IAM authentication (not passwords)
- [ ] One DDL statement per transaction
- [ ] Use `CREATE INDEX ASYNC` (never synchronous)
- [ ] Store arrays/JSON as TEXT columns
- [ ] Implement referential integrity in application code
- [ ] Batch operations under 3,000 rows
- [ ] Use DSQL Connector library when available for your language

### Multi-Tenant Pattern (DSQL)

```sql
-- Schema-per-tenant for strong isolation
CREATE SCHEMA tenant_abc;
CREATE TABLE tenant_abc.orders (
  id UUID DEFAULT gen_random_uuid() PRIMARY KEY,
  tenant_id TEXT NOT NULL,
  product TEXT NOT NULL,
  amount NUMERIC(10,2) NOT NULL,
  created_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT now()
);
CREATE INDEX ASYNC ON tenant_abc.orders (tenant_id);
```

## Step 6: Caching Patterns

### Cache-Aside (Lazy Loading)

```
1. Check cache (ElastiCache)
2. If miss → query database
3. Write result to cache with TTL
4. Return result
```

### Write-Through

```
1. Write to database
2. Write to cache
3. Return result
```

### Cache Invalidation Strategy

| Pattern | When to Use | Complexity |
|---|---|---|
| TTL-based | Read-heavy, eventual consistency OK | Low |
| Write-through | Strong consistency needed | Medium |
| Event-driven (DynamoDB Streams → Lambda → cache) | Real-time invalidation | Medium |
| Cache-aside + short TTL | Balance of freshness and simplicity | Low |

## Step 7: Migration Planning

### Migration Checklist

- [ ] Inventory current schema, data volume, access patterns
- [ ] Map source types to target types
- [ ] Plan for downtime window or zero-downtime migration
- [ ] Test migration on copy of production data
- [ ] Validate row counts and data integrity post-migration
- [ ] Update connection strings and ORM configs
- [ ] Run application integration tests against new database
- [ ] Plan rollback procedure

### Common Migration Paths

| From | To | Tool |
|---|---|---|
| MySQL/PostgreSQL (self-hosted) | Aurora | AWS DMS |
| MongoDB | DocumentDB | AWS DMS |
| Cassandra | Keyspaces | AWS DMS |
| PostgreSQL | Aurora DSQL | Manual (schema + data) |
| DynamoDB → DynamoDB (cross-account) | DynamoDB | AWS Backup or export/import |

## Report

A reviewer writes each row as a finding (`write_findings`); a builder puts the summary in its finish.

```
## Database Review: [target]

### Current Stack: [database] + [ORM] + [compute]
### Summary: X MUST / Y SHOULD / Z NIT

| # | Category | Check | Status | Details |
|---|----------|-------|--------|---------|
```

## Self-Check

- [ ] Database choice matches access patterns (not just familiarity)
- [ ] Connection management appropriate for compute type
- [ ] Encryption enabled (at rest and in transit)
- [ ] Backup/recovery configured (PITR, snapshots)
- [ ] Multi-tenant isolation enforced
- [ ] No N+1 query patterns
- [ ] Indexes match query patterns
- [ ] Migration plan includes rollback

For security hardening, see the `aws-security` skill.
For performance profiling, see the `perf-debug` skill.
For database selection details, see `references/selection-guide.md`.
For DynamoDB advanced patterns, see `references/dynamodb-patterns.md`.
For Aurora DSQL specifics, see `references/dsql-guide.md`.
For verified sources on claims in this skill, see `references/sources.md`.

The run writes migrations and their rollback as code and tests them against what the sandbox can run (an in-memory
or local engine); applying one to a real database is a person's step after the merge.

# Databases on AWS: Aurora DSQL Guide

## What is Aurora DSQL

Aurora DSQL is a serverless, PostgreSQL-compatible distributed SQL database. It provides:
- Serverless scaling (no capacity planning)
- Multi-region active-active
- PostgreSQL wire protocol compatibility
- IAM-based authentication
- Optimistic concurrency control (OCC)

## Key Constraints

| Constraint | Limit | Workaround |
|---|---|---|
| Max rows per transaction | 3,000 | Batch operations |
| Max data per transaction | 10 MiB | Split large writes |
| Max transaction duration | 5 min | Break into smaller transactions |
| Max connections | 10,000 | Connection pooling |
| Max connection duration | 60 min | Reconnect periodically |
| IAM auth token expiry | 15 min | Use the language connector for auto-refresh |
| Max indexes per table | 24 | Prioritize query patterns |
| Max columns per index | 8 | Composite indexes |
| Foreign keys | Not supported | Application-layer enforcement |
| ALTER COLUMN TYPE | Not supported | Table recreation pattern |
| DROP COLUMN | Not supported | Table recreation pattern |
| Synchronous CREATE INDEX | Not supported | Use CREATE INDEX ASYNC |
| IDENTITY/SEQUENCE CACHE | 1 or >= 65536 | Plan for gaps |

## DDL Rules

### One DDL Per Transaction

```sql
-- CORRECT: separate transactions
BEGIN; CREATE TABLE orders (...); COMMIT;
BEGIN; CREATE INDEX ASYNC idx_orders_status ON orders (status); COMMIT;

-- WRONG: multiple DDL in one transaction
BEGIN;
CREATE TABLE orders (...);
CREATE INDEX ASYNC idx_orders_status ON orders (status);  -- Will fail
COMMIT;
```

### CREATE INDEX ASYNC

Always use ASYNC for index creation:

```sql
-- CORRECT
CREATE INDEX ASYNC idx_orders_tenant ON orders (tenant_id);

-- WRONG (will fail or block)
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_tenant ON orders (tenant_id);
```

Check index status:
```sql
SELECT * FROM pg_stat_all_indexes WHERE indexrelname = 'idx_orders_tenant';
```

## Table Recreation Pattern

For operations DSQL doesn't support (ALTER COLUMN TYPE, DROP COLUMN, DROP CONSTRAINT):

```sql
-- Step 1: Create new table with desired schema
CREATE TABLE orders_new (
  id UUID DEFAULT gen_random_uuid() PRIMARY KEY,
  tenant_id TEXT NOT NULL,
  amount NUMERIC(12,2) NOT NULL,  -- Changed from NUMERIC(10,2)
  created_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT now()
);

-- Step 2: Copy data in batches (max 3,000 rows per transaction)
INSERT INTO orders_new (id, tenant_id, amount, created_at)
SELECT id, tenant_id, amount::NUMERIC(12,2), created_at
FROM orders
ORDER BY id
LIMIT 3000 OFFSET 0;
-- Repeat with increasing OFFSET until all rows copied

-- Step 3: Verify row counts match
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders;
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders_new;

-- Step 4: Swap tables
DROP TABLE orders;
ALTER TABLE orders_new RENAME TO orders;

-- Step 5: Recreate indexes (separate transactions)
CREATE INDEX ASYNC idx_orders_tenant ON orders (tenant_id);
```

## Connection Patterns

### IAM Authentication

```python
import boto3

def get_dsql_token(cluster_endpoint: str, region: str) -> str:
    client = boto3.client('dsql', region_name=region)
    return client.generate_db_connect_auth_token(
        Hostname=cluster_endpoint,
        Region=region,
        ExpiresIn=900  # 15 minutes max
    )
```

### Language-Specific Drivers

| Language | Recommended Driver | DSQL Connector |
|---|---|---|
| Python | psycopg2 / asyncpg | aurora-dsql-python |
| TypeScript/JS | pg (node-postgres) | aurora-dsql-js |
| Go | pgx | aurora-dsql-go |
| Java | JDBC PostgreSQL | aurora-dsql-java |
| Rust | tokio-postgres | aurora-dsql-rust |

Prefer the DSQL Connector when available, because it handles IAM token refresh and connection management.
Bare drivers (`pg`, `psycopg2`, `pgx`) work until the first 15-minute token expiry, then every new
connection fails auth. Use the Connector or implement token refresh yourself before shipping.

## Multi-Tenant Patterns

### Schema-Per-Tenant (Strong Isolation)

```sql
-- Create tenant schema
CREATE SCHEMA tenant_abc;

-- Create tables in tenant schema
CREATE TABLE tenant_abc.orders (
  id UUID DEFAULT gen_random_uuid() PRIMARY KEY,
  product TEXT NOT NULL,
  amount NUMERIC(10,2) NOT NULL
);

-- Grant access to tenant role
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA tenant_abc TO role_tenant_abc;
GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA tenant_abc TO role_tenant_abc;
```

### Shared Table with Tenant Column (Cost-Efficient)

```sql
CREATE TABLE orders (
  id UUID DEFAULT gen_random_uuid() PRIMARY KEY,
  tenant_id TEXT NOT NULL,
  product TEXT NOT NULL,
  amount NUMERIC(10,2) NOT NULL
);
CREATE INDEX ASYNC idx_orders_tenant ON orders (tenant_id);

-- Include tenant_id in every query (it scopes the row to one tenant)
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE tenant_id = 'abc' AND amount > 100;
```

**Rules:**
- Include `tenant_id` in every WHERE clause, because a query without it reads across tenants; build it with
  parameter binding (`$1`), never string interpolation
- Authorize the caller against that `tenant_id` before querying. Format validation (regex,
  allowlist) alone is not authorization: a well-formed `tenant_id` the caller doesn't own is
  still a cross-tenant leak
- When `psql -c` or any other raw-SQL path is unavoidable, validate every untrusted value with
  a dedicated check per kind: allowlist/regex for values, identifier-grammar check for
  table/column names, membership check for sort direction keywords (`ASC`/`DESC`)

## Application-Layer Referential Integrity

Since DSQL doesn't support foreign keys:

```python
async def create_order_item(order_id: str, item_data: dict):
    # Step 1: Verify parent exists
    result = await query("SELECT id FROM orders WHERE id = $1", order_id)
    if not result:
        raise ValueError(f"Order {order_id} not found")

    # Step 2: Insert child
    await execute(
        "INSERT INTO order_items (order_id, product, quantity) VALUES ($1, $2, $3)",
        order_id, item_data['product'], item_data['quantity']
    )

async def delete_order(order_id: str):
    # Step 1: Check for dependents
    count = await query("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM order_items WHERE order_id = $1", order_id)
    if count > 0:
        raise ValueError(f"Order {order_id} has {count} items, delete them first")

    # Step 2: Delete parent
    await execute("DELETE FROM orders WHERE id = $1", order_id)
```

## Troubleshooting

| Error | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| OCC serialization error | Concurrent writes to same row | Retry transaction; reduce contention |
| Transaction too large | >3,000 rows or >10 MiB | Split into smaller batches |
| Connection refused | Token expired or wrong endpoint | Refresh IAM token |
| Index creation stuck | ASYNC index still building | Check pg_stat_all_indexes; wait |
| ALTER COLUMN TYPE failed | Not supported in DSQL | Use table recreation pattern |
| Foreign key error | Not supported in DSQL | Implement in application code |

# Databases on AWS: Selection Guide

## Decision Flowchart

```
What's your primary access pattern?
│
├─ Key-value lookups (get by ID, simple queries)
│  └─ Need <10ms latency at any scale? → DynamoDB
│
├─ Complex SQL queries (joins, aggregations, transactions)
│  ├─ Need serverless + multi-region? → Aurora DSQL
│  ├─ Need PostgreSQL/MySQL compatibility? → Aurora Serverless v2
│  └─ Need specific engine (Oracle, SQL Server)? → RDS
│
├─ Document store (flexible schema, nested objects)
│  └─ MongoDB-compatible? → DocumentDB
│
├─ Caching / session store
│  └─ Sub-millisecond latency? → ElastiCache (Redis/Valkey)
│
├─ Full-text search / log analytics
│  └─ Search + dashboards? → OpenSearch
│
├─ Graph relationships (social, fraud, knowledge)
│  └─ Traversal queries? → Neptune
│
├─ Time-series (IoT, metrics, events)
│  └─ Time-based queries + retention? → Timestream
│
└─ Immutable ledger (audit, compliance)
   └─ QLDB support ended 31 July 2025. Use Aurora PostgreSQL, append-only
      with a cryptographic hash chain, instead
```

## Detailed Comparison

### DynamoDB vs Aurora

| Dimension | DynamoDB | Aurora Serverless v2 |
|---|---|---|
| Data model | Key-value / document | Relational (SQL) |
| Query flexibility | Limited (design for access patterns) | Full SQL (joins, subqueries) |
| Scaling | Automatic, unlimited | Auto-scaling ACUs (0.5–128) |
| Latency | Single-digit ms | Low ms (varies with query) |
| Transactions | 100 items, 4MB | Full ACID |
| Cost model | Per-request or provisioned | Per-ACU-hour |
| Schema changes | Flexible (schemaless) | Requires migrations |
| Best for | High-scale, simple access patterns | Complex queries, existing SQL apps |

### Aurora Serverless v2 vs Aurora DSQL

| Dimension | Aurora Serverless v2 | Aurora DSQL |
|---|---|---|
| Compatibility | PostgreSQL or MySQL | PostgreSQL (subset) |
| Distribution | Single-region, multi-AZ | Multi-region |
| Scaling | ACU-based (0.5–128) | Fully serverless |
| Foreign keys | Yes | No (application-layer) |
| ALTER COLUMN TYPE | Yes | No (table recreation) |
| Max transaction | Standard PostgreSQL | 3,000 rows / 10 MiB |
| Authentication | Password or IAM | IAM only |
| Best for | Standard relational workloads | Distributed, serverless SQL |

### DynamoDB vs ElastiCache

| Dimension | DynamoDB | ElastiCache |
|---|---|---|
| Latency | Single-digit ms | Sub-millisecond |
| Persistence | Durable (replicated) | Optional (snapshots) |
| Data model | Key-value / document | Key-value, sorted sets, streams |
| Scaling | Automatic | Manual (node types) |
| Cost | Per-request | Per-node-hour |
| Best for | Primary data store | Cache layer, session store, leaderboards |

## When NOT to Use Each Service

| Service | Don't Use When |
|---|---|
| DynamoDB | You need complex joins, ad-hoc queries, or full-text search |
| Aurora | You have simple key-value access and need unlimited scale |
| Aurora DSQL | You need foreign keys, complex DDL, or MySQL compatibility |
| DocumentDB | You need strong consistency or complex transactions |
| ElastiCache | You need durable primary storage |
| OpenSearch | You need ACID transactions or strong consistency |
| Neptune | Your relationships are simple (use DynamoDB GSIs instead) |
| Timestream | You need general-purpose queries beyond time-series |

## Multi-Database Architectures

### Common Combinations

| Primary | Secondary | Pattern |
|---|---|---|
| DynamoDB | ElastiCache | Cache hot items, reduce read costs |
| Aurora | ElastiCache | Cache query results, session store |
| DynamoDB | OpenSearch | DynamoDB for writes, OpenSearch for search |
| Aurora | DynamoDB | Aurora for transactions, DynamoDB for high-scale reads |

### Data Sync Patterns

| Source | Target | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| DynamoDB | OpenSearch | DynamoDB Streams → Lambda → OpenSearch |
| DynamoDB | ElastiCache | DynamoDB Streams → Lambda → ElastiCache |
| Aurora | ElastiCache | Application-level write-through or CDC |
| S3 | DynamoDB | S3 event → Lambda → DynamoDB |

## Sizing Guidelines (Dev)

| Service | Dev Config | Est. Monthly |
|---|---|---|
| DynamoDB | On-demand, <1GB | $1–5 |
| Aurora Serverless v2 | 0.5 min ACU, 10GB | $45–60 |
| Aurora DSQL | Serverless, light | $10–20 |
| ElastiCache | cache.t3.micro | $12 |
| DocumentDB | db.t3.medium | $55 |
| OpenSearch | t3.small.search, 1 node | $25 |
| Neptune | db.t3.medium | $55 |
| Timestream | On-demand, <1GB | $5–10 |

# Sources

Non-obvious claims verified against AWS documentation and the official AWS `aurora-dsql`
agent skill (via `aws___retrieve_skill`). Checked 2026-10-28.

| Claim | Source | Checked |
|---|---|---|
| Aurora DSQL limits: 3,000 rows/transaction, 10 MiB/transaction, 24 indexes/table, 8 columns/index, 10,000 connections/cluster | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/aurora-dsql/latest/userguide/CHAP_quotas.html | 2026-10-28 |
| Aurora DSQL max connection duration 60 min, IAM auth token expiry 15 min | official `aurora-dsql` AWS agent skill (`aws___retrieve_skill`) | 2026-10-28 |
| Bare Postgres drivers (no DSQL Connector) fail auth on every new connection after the first 15-minute token expiry | official `aurora-dsql` AWS agent skill (`aws___retrieve_skill`) | 2026-10-28 |
| `boto3.client('dsql').generate_db_connect_auth_token(...)` is a real, current API | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/boto3/latest/reference/services/dsql/client/generate_db_connect_admin_auth_token.html | 2026-10-28 |
| QLDB reached end of support; no new ledger workloads should target it | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cdk/api/v1/java/software/amazon/awscdk/services/qldb/package-summary.html (deprecated), cross-checked against the AWS QLDB migration guidance | 2026-10-28 |
| Aurora Serverless v2 ACU range, DynamoDB transaction/batch limits (100 items/4MB transact, 25/16MB batch write, 100/16MB batch get) | existing AWS SDK/API docs, unchanged since last review | 2026-10-28 |

---
name: deploy-agentcore
description: "Writes the infrastructure and code for an agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime: the stable CDK L2, ARM64 image builds, least-privilege IAM. Read it when writing AgentCore IaC, its build pipeline or its smoke test; the deploy itself is a person's."
source: "ai-skill-factory 2.0.0 (Amit Deol), skills/deploy-agentcore"
license: MIT
adapted: "The run never builds, pushes or deploys: the image build, the dependency-ordered deploy and the live smoke test became code the agent writes (the build pipeline, the stack, the smoke-test script) and steps its finish hands to a person, in order. Validation is offline (cdk synth and tests). Discovery uses run's grep and read_file. The report is the finish summary; description and emphasis reworded for Claude 5.5 skill discovery"
---

Write the infrastructure and code that put the agent your task names on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime.

If your task names no path, find the agent entrypoint (`agent.py` / `app.py` with `BedrockAgentCoreApp`) and the
CDK stack directory with `list_files` and `read_file`.

The run never builds an image, pushes one or deploys: the sandbox has no Docker, no network and no AWS account.
You write the stack, the build pipeline's code and the smoke test, validate them offline (`cdk synth`, the tests),
and your finish lists what a person runs, in order (Steps 6 and 7).

## Step 1: Confirm Construct and Tooling Choice

AgentCore has three deployment surfaces. Pick one and do not mix them.

| Surface | Module / Tool | Status | Use when |
|---|---|---|---|
| Stable CDK L2 | `aws_cdk.aws_bedrockagentcore` (ships **inside** `aws-cdk-lib`) | **Current - use this** | You own a CDK app and want IaC review/diff/rollback |
| Alpha CDK L2 | `aws_cdk.aws_bedrock_agentcore_alpha` (separate pip pkg) | **DEPRECATED** | Never for new code - migrate off it |
| AgentCore CLI | `@aws/agentcore` (npm, CDK-backed) | Current | Quickstart / no existing CDK app |
| Starter toolkit | `bedrock-agentcore-starter-toolkit` (pip) | **DEPRECATED** | Never for new projects |

**Default: stable CDK L2.** The alpha module and the stable in-library module share an identical API surface, so migration is a one-line import swap. See `references/cdk-constructs.md` for the verified API and the migration diff.

If the project has no CDK app and the task asks for the fastest path, the `@aws/agentcore` npm CLI is the
alternative (`agentcore create` then `agentcore deploy`, a person's commands); it is CDK-backed under the hood.

## Step 2: Validate the Agent Entrypoint

The container must expose the AgentCore contract or deployment fails at runtime.

- [ ] Entrypoint uses `BedrockAgentCoreApp` with an `@app.entrypoint` handler
- [ ] Handler signature is `def handler(payload: dict) -> dict | str` (or async)
- [ ] `app.run()` is the module's `__main__` (binds `0.0.0.0:8080`, serves `/invocations` + `/ping`)
- [ ] No reliance on local files written at request time - sessions run in ephemeral microVMs
- [ ] Long work tolerates the per-request timeout; stream when the protocol is HTTP

Find them with `run` `["grep", "-rn", "-e", "BedrockAgentCoreApp", "-e", "@app.entrypoint", "-e", "app.run()", "<agent dir>"]`.

## Step 3: The ARM64 Image Build (code you write, a build a person runs)

AgentCore Runtime runs **ARM64 (Graviton)** containers. A non-ARM64 image fails with `exec format error`. Prefer AWS CodeBuild: it removes the cross-architecture question entirely. Building locally is acceptable only on an arm64 host that can push to ECR, and emulated `--platform linux/arm64` builds on x86 are slow and a common source of silent failures.

Build flow (S3 source upload → CodeBuild ARM64 → ECR push):
1. Zip the agent source dir.
2. Upload to the CodeBuild source bucket.
3. Run the CodeBuild project (buildspec does `docker build --platform linux/arm64`, pushes `:$GIT_SHA` and `:latest`).
4. Capture the immutable `:$GIT_SHA` image URI - pass that to CDK, not `:latest`.

The build is driven from the project's own deploy script (illustrated as `scripts/deploy_codebuild.py`); when the
task asks for one, write it. `references/build-pipeline.md` gives the full buildspec and boto3 calls. A person runs
it (`python scripts/deploy_codebuild.py --skip-deploy` builds the image only and prints its URI).

`CodeZip` (S3 zip, no Docker anywhere) is AWS's default/recommended build type for simple agents. Use a `Container` build when you need system packages, large binaries, or a custom runtime. See `references/build-pipeline.md`.

## Step 4: Wire the Stable CDK Runtime Construct

Minimum viable runtime, IAM auth, public network, ECR image built in Step 3:

```python
from aws_cdk.aws_bedrockagentcore import (
    AgentRuntimeArtifact, ProtocolType, Runtime,
    RuntimeAuthorizerConfiguration, RuntimeNetworkConfiguration,
)

runtime = Runtime(
    self, "AgentRuntime",
    runtime_name=f"agent_eval_runtime_{env_name}",
    agent_runtime_artifact=AgentRuntimeArtifact.from_image_uri(image_uri),
    execution_role=execution_role,                     # pre-created, Step 5
    authorizer_configuration=RuntimeAuthorizerConfiguration.using_iam(),
    network_configuration=RuntimeNetworkConfiguration.using_public_network(),
    protocol_configuration=ProtocolType.HTTP,
)
endpoint = runtime.add_endpoint(f"agent_eval_endpoint_{env_name}")
```

- `from_image_uri` does **not** auto-grant ECR pull - grant it explicitly (Step 5).
- Authorizer options: `using_iam()`, `using_cognito(pool, [client])`, `using_jwt(...)`, `using_o_auth(...)`. Never leave a runtime unauthenticated.
- The `DEFAULT` endpoint auto-tracks the latest version. For blue/green, add a named endpoint pinned to a version. See `references/cdk-constructs.md`.

## Step 5: Apply the Security Gate (mandatory, in the code you submit)

AgentCore Runtime is internet-reachable, so the auth gate applies to the stack before anyone deploys it. All must
be YES:

- [ ] Authorizer set (IAM / Cognito / JWT) - no unauthenticated runtime endpoint
- [ ] Execution role trust policy carries confused-deputy guards: `aws:SourceAccount == this.account` **and** `aws:SourceArn` ArnLike `arn:aws:bedrock-agentcore:{region}:{account}:runtime/*`
- [ ] `bedrock:InvokeModel*` scoped to specific model / inference-profile ARNs - never `Resource: "*"`
- [ ] ECR pull granted to the exec role for the exact repo (`ecr_repo.grant_pull(execution_role)`)
- [ ] Data-store grants (S3 / DynamoDB) scoped to named resource ARNs, least-privilege
- [ ] Logs scoped to `/aws/bedrock-agentcore/runtimes/*`; X-Ray + `cloudwatch:PutMetricData` gated by namespace condition
- [ ] Two-role split: a CodeBuild service role (build) distinct from the runtime execution role (run)

If any answer is NO, **fix it before you submit.** Full role policies in `references/iam-security.md`. Sources for the AWS-specific facts in this skill: `references/sources.md`.

## Step 6: The Deploy Order (a person's, listed in your finish)

A person deploys, in dependency order:

```bash
GIT_SHA=$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)
IMAGE_URI="$ACCOUNT.dkr.ecr.$REGION.amazonaws.com/agent-eval-runtime:$GIT_SHA"
JSII_SILENCE_WARNING_UNTESTED_NODE_VERSION=1 \
  npx aws-cdk deploy <stacks> --require-approval never \
  -c environment=$ENV -c agent_image_uri=$IMAGE_URI
```

**CloudFormation export-ordering trap:** when you remove a cross-stack export that a deployed consumer still imports, `--all` ordering fails with *"Cannot delete export ... as it is in use."* Deploy the **consumer stack first** (`cdk deploy <consumer> --exclusively`) to drop the import, then deploy the producer. See `references/build-pipeline.md`.

Versioning recap: `CreateAgentRuntime` → v1 + DEFAULT endpoint; every `UpdateAgentRuntime` mints a new immutable version; DEFAULT auto-advances, named endpoints pin. Always tag images by commit SHA so old versions keep their images.

## Step 7: The Smoke Test (written by you, run by a person)

The live runtime is invoked end-to-end after the deploy, by the project's smoke-test script (shown as
`scripts/post_deploy_eval.py`; `references/build-pipeline.md` gives the `bedrock-agentcore` invoke call). When the
task asks for one, write it and unit-test its parsing offline; a person runs it:

```bash
python scripts/post_deploy_eval.py --runtime-arn "$RUNTIME_ARN" --region "$REGION"
```

- `runtimeSessionId` must be 33 to 256 chars.
- Use backend-independent smoke cases (e.g. a greeting + a safety check) so the test isn't gated on data fixtures.
- Confirm CloudWatch alarms/dashboard exist and the runtime reached `READY`/`ACTIVE`.
- Gate on the result: `all_passed: true` before promoting a named endpoint.

## Step 8: Report

Put this in your `finish` summary (the live fields are a person's to fill after their deploy):

```
## AgentCore Deployment Report

Runtime ARN:   <arn>
Image:         <repo>:<git-sha>   (ARM64, CodeBuild)
Construct:     aws_cdk.aws_bedrockagentcore (stable L2)
Auth:          IAM | Cognito | JWT
Security gate: PASS (8/8)
Smoke test:    all_passed=<bool>  (<n> cases)
Stacks:        <list> - all *_COMPLETE
Endpoints:     DEFAULT -> v<n>; <named> -> v<n>
```

Flag any UNVERIFIED assumption and any security-gate item that was waived. Gates you ran: `cdk synth` and the
tests, with their exit codes; the deploy, the smoke test and the endpoint promotion are a person's.
