# Doc Plan: Canonical Understanding-Doc Set

The file set the planner schedules and the `understand-docs` skill describes how to write. On the platform it is the
shape the understander's draft takes; the files below are what a person's docs pull request would hold. Based on C4 + arc42 (the c4model.com FAQ documents this pairing). Single source of truth: each fact lives in one file; others link.

## File tree

```
project-review-understanding-document/
  REVIEW-PLAN.md            # the plan (the understand-plan skill, Step 5); the generation contract
  _model/                   # the extracted model (on the platform: the mapper's notes)
  docs/
    INDEX.md                # master registry: what exists, audience, level, last-verified
    00-overview.md          # L100  C4 System Context  / arc42 §1, §3
    01-containers.md        # L200  C4 Container        / arc42 §5-L1
    02-components.md        # L300  C4 Component        / arc42 §5-L2
    03-deployment.md        # L400  C4 Deployment       / arc42 §7
    04-solution-strategy.md # L200  (prose)             / arc42 §4 (+ §1 goals)
    05-crosscutting.md      # L400  (prose)             / arc42 §8
    06-adrs/                # MADR records              / arc42 §9
      0001-<decision>.md
    07-risks.md             # signals + tech debt       / arc42 §11
    08-glossary.md          # term definitions          / arc42 §12
    09-dynamic/             # L300 runtime flows         / arc42 §6 (only if complex)
      <flow-name>.md
```

## File responsibilities: single source of truth

| File | Owns (lives only here) | Must not repeat |
|---|---|---|
| `00-overview.md` | External actors, system boundary, external systems | Internal containers |
| `01-containers.md` | Stacks/apps-as-containers, AWS service boxes, cross-stack wiring | How they deploy (-> 03) |
| `02-components.md` | Internal modules, Pulumi ComponentResource / CDK Construct classes, interfaces | Cross-stack wiring (-> 01) |
| `03-deployment.md` | Environments, VPC/subnet layout, instance config, CI/CD runtime | Static responsibilities (-> 01) |
| `04-solution-strategy.md` | Why Pulumi/CDK + language, why SageMaker/Bedrock, quality tradeoffs | ADR rationale (link -> 06) |
| `05-crosscutting.md` | IAM model, tagging, secrets, encryption, model governance, observability | Per-component logic (-> 02) |
| `06-adrs/` | Decision rationale, options, consequences | Restating what (link from 04) |
| `07-risks.md` | Unresolved risks, tech debt, security/cost/reliability signals | Resolved decisions (-> 06) |
| `08-glossary.md` | Canonical term definitions | Usage examples (link) |
| `INDEX.md` | The registry mapping the whole set | File-local scope (each file states its own) |

## Anti-duplication rules

1. Each fact in exactly one file; others link with a relative path.
2. Diagrams are authoritative; prose describes the diagram, never restates its structure.
3. `04-solution-strategy.md` links to ADRs; it does not restate their rationale.
4. Container diagram (L200) excludes load balancers and replica counts; those belong in deployment (L400).
5. Glossary owns definitions; elsewhere use the term + link, never redefine inline.
6. `INDEX.md` owns the registry; each doc states only its own scope.

## arc42 priority for IaC/AI projects

| arc42 § | Priority | Maps to file |
|---|---|---|
| §3 Context & Scope | HIGH | 00-overview |
| §4 Solution Strategy | HIGH | 04-solution-strategy |
| §5 Building Block | HIGH | 01-containers (L1), 02-components (L2) |
| §6 Runtime | MEDIUM (key flows only) | 09-dynamic |
| §7 Deployment | CRITICAL | 03-deployment |
| §8 Crosscutting | HIGH | 05-crosscutting |
| §9 Decisions | HIGH | 06-adrs |
| §11 Risks | MEDIUM | 07-risks |
| §12 Glossary | MEDIUM | 08-glossary |
| §1 Goals, §2 Constraints | MEDIUM | folded into 00 / 04 |
| §10 Quality | LOW | brief list in 04; skip full quality tree |

C4 Level 4 (code diagrams) is skipped: IaC is declarative; class-level diagrams add no value beyond the optional Pulumi-component / CDK-construct `classDiagram` at L400.

## ADR detection (MADR format)

Capture significant, alternatives-bearing decisions. Common candidates in Pulumi/CDK/AI-on-AWS repos:
- IaC tool (Pulumi vs CDK vs Terraform) and language (TS vs Python vs Go vs Java)
- Training platform (SageMaker vs Batch vs EC2) and serving (Bedrock vs SageMaker endpoint vs ECS)
- Vector store (OpenSearch Serverless vs Aurora pgvector vs external)
- Agent approach (Bedrock Agents vs AgentCore vs custom framework)
- State/synth model (Pulumi backend: Cloud vs S3; CDK: bootstrap + CloudFormation), secrets provider, multi-stack decomposition

One decision per ADR. Status field required. Append-only (supersede, never edit history).

## Markers the planner records per doc

For each file, the REVIEW-PLAN records: applicable (yes/skip + reason), level, the Mermaid diagram type(s), the model element ids feeding each diagram, and any open question blocking generation.

# Extraction Reference: Surveying a Pulumi or CDK / AI-on-AWS Project

How to extract an accurate, provenance-tagged model without deploying. On the platform the mapper and the
understander run no command: they take Tier 3 (source files) and any committed `cdk.out/` (Tier 2) with
`read_file` and `list_files`, and write the model as notes. The commands below are for a person's survey, or a role
that runs code; the `_model/` files are the source method's, which the notes replace. Static-first, optional state/synth export. Read-only against infrastructure. Works for two IaC tools: Pulumi (state export) and AWS CDK (CloudFormation synth). Detect the tool from marker files (`Pulumi.yaml` vs `cdk.json`), then follow the matching phase. A repo may use both.

## Safe vs unsafe commands (Pulumi)

| Command | Needs | Safe? | Use |
|---|---|---|---|
| `find . -name "Pulumi.yaml"` | nothing | YES | Project inventory |
| `grep -rn "new aws\."` | nothing | YES | Resource instantiation scan |
| `pulumi about` | backend login | YES (read) | Runtime, providers, backend |
| `pulumi stack ls` | backend login | YES (read) | Stack inventory |
| `pulumi stack --show-urns` | backend login | YES (read) | URN tree |
| `pulumi config` | backend login | YES (read) | Config keys (secrets stay ciphertext) |
| `pulumi stack export` | backend login | YES (read) | Full state JSON. NO AWS creds needed |
| `pulumi stack graph --file g.dot` | backend login | YES (read) | Dependency DOT graph |
| `pulumi preview --json` | AWS creds | read-only, OPTIONAL, a person's | Drift vs live cloud |
| `pulumi refresh` | AWS creds | NO during audit | Mutates state file |
| `pulumi up` / `pulumi destroy` | AWS creds | NEVER | Mutates / deletes infra |

State lives in the Pulumi backend (Pulumi Cloud, S3, local), not the cloud account. `pulumi stack export` reads state, not AWS, so it needs no cloud credentials and reveals no live secrets.

## Safe vs unsafe commands (CDK)

| Command | Needs | Safe? | Use |
|---|---|---|---|
| `find . -name "cdk.json"` | nothing | YES | App inventory |
| `grep -rn "new s3.Bucket\|extends Stack"` | nothing | YES | Construct/stack scan |
| `cdk ls` | nothing (offline) | YES (read) | Stack inventory in the app |
| `cdk synth` / `cdk synth --quiet` | nothing (offline) | YES (read) | Expand constructs to CloudFormation templates in `cdk.out/` |
| read `cdk.out/*.template.json` | nothing | YES | Synthesized resources, logical IDs, deps |
| read `cdk.out/manifest.json`, `tree.json` | nothing | YES | Stack list, construct tree, dependencies |
| `cdk diff` | AWS creds | read-only, OPTIONAL, a person's | Drift vs deployed stack |
| `aws cloudformation get-template` | AWS creds | read-only, OPTIONAL, a person's | Deployed template (Tier 1) |
| `cdk deploy` / `cdk destroy` | AWS creds | NEVER | Mutates / deletes infra |

`cdk synth` runs locally and needs no AWS credentials. It is the CDK equivalent of Pulumi state export for accuracy: it expands every L2/L3 construct (which hide many resources) into concrete CloudFormation. Prefer reading `cdk.out` templates over grepping construct calls. If `cdk synth` fails (missing deps, bootstrap context), fall back to reading any committed `cdk.out/` then to source grep, and record the lower tier.

## Phase 1 (Pulumi): Static read (zero credentials)

1. **Projects**: `find "$TARGET" -name "Pulumi.yaml" -not -path "*/node_modules/*" | sort`. Each = one project. Read `name`, `runtime`, `description`.
2. **Stacks**: `find "$TARGET" -name "Pulumi.*.yaml" | grep -v "/Pulumi.yaml" | sort`. Each = one stack (dev/staging/prod, regional splits).
3. **Config intent**: parse each `Pulumi.<stack>.yaml` `config:` block. Keys reveal region, instance types, model IDs, feature flags. `secure:` keys are encrypted; the KEY NAME documents intent (e.g., `dbPassword`). Never decrypt.
4. **Provider packages**: read `package.json` / `requirements.txt` / `go.mod`. Presence of `awsx`, `pulumi-eks` sets the component vocabulary to expect.
5. **Resource instantiations** (record `file:line` for each):
   ```bash
   grep -rn "new aws\.\|new awsx\.\|new eks\." --include="*.ts" "$TARGET"
   grep -rn "aws\.\w\+\.\w\+(" --include="*.py" "$TARGET"
   grep -rn "^[[:space:]]*type: aws" --include="*.yaml" "$TARGET"
   grep -rn "NewBucket\|NewFunction\|sagemaker\.\|bedrock\." --include="*.go" "$TARGET"
   ```
6. **Stack references** (inter-project edges): `grep -rn "StackReference" "$TARGET"`. Parse `"org/project/stack"`.
7. **Components**: `grep -rn "ComponentResource" --include="*.ts" --include="*.py" "$TARGET"`. Read each constructor to enumerate child resources.
8. **Exports** (what a project exposes): `grep -rn "pulumi.export\|export const" "$TARGET"`.
9. **Module graph** (for L200): if tools present, use `madge --json` (TS), `grimp`/`pydeps` (Python), `go mod graph` (Go). Else derive from import statements.

## Phase 2 (Pulumi): State export (backend login, no AWS creds), Tier 1 only

```bash
pulumi stack select <stack>
pulumi stack export > _model/state-<stack>.json
jq '[.deployment.resources[].type] | unique | sort' _model/state-<stack>.json   # type inventory
jq '.deployment.resources[] | {urn,type,id,parent,deps:.dependencies}' _model/state-<stack>.json
```

State resource fields to extract: `urn` (parse `urn:pulumi:<stack>::<project>::<type>::<name>`), `type` (-> AWS service), `inputs` (real sizes/ARNs/env incl. model IDs), `parent` (component tree), `dependencies` (edges). State `urn` is the strongest provenance; prefer it over `file:line` when both exist.

## Phase 1 (CDK): Static read + synth (zero credentials)

1. **Apps**: `find "$TARGET" -name "cdk.json" -not -path "*/node_modules/*" | sort`. Each = one CDK app. Read `cdk.json` `app` (entrypoint + language), `context` (env, feature flags).
2. **Language + deps**: read `package.json` / `requirements.txt` / `pom.xml` / `go.mod`. CDK language sets the construct vocabulary (`aws-cdk-lib`, `constructs`, `@aws-cdk/aws-*` alpha modules).
3. **Synthesize** (preferred, offline): `cd "$TARGET" && cdk synth --quiet` writes `cdk.out/`. If it fails, use any committed `cdk.out/`, else fall back to source grep (record the tier).
4. **Stack inventory**: `cdk ls` or read `cdk.out/manifest.json` `artifacts` (type `aws:cloudformation:stack`). Each = one CloudFormation stack.
5. **Construct tree**: read `cdk.out/tree.json` for the construct hierarchy (app -> stacks -> L3/L2/L1 constructs). This is the CDK analog of the Pulumi component tree.
6. **Resource scan from source** (record `file:line` for each construct call):
   ```bash
   grep -rn "extends Stack\|extends Construct" --include="*.ts" "$TARGET"
   grep -rn "new \(s3\|lambda\|dynamodb\|apigateway\|sfn\|sns\|sqs\|ec2\|rds\|ecs\|iam\|kms\|cognito\|bedrock\|sagemaker\)\." --include="*.ts" "$TARGET"
   grep -rn "Stack)\|Construct)" --include="*.py" "$TARGET"        # Python: class X(Stack)
   grep -rn "aws_cdk\|from constructs" --include="*.py" "$TARGET"
   ```
7. **Cross-stack edges**: stack-to-stack property passes in app code (constructor args), plus synthesized `Fn::ImportValue` / `Export` pairs in templates. `grep -rn "Fn::ImportValue\|\"Export\"" cdk.out/`.
8. **CfnOutput** (what a stack exposes): `grep -rn "new CfnOutput\|CfnOutput(" "$TARGET"` and `Outputs` blocks in `cdk.out/*.template.json`.
9. **Module graph** (for L200): if tools present, `madge --json` (TS), `grimp`/`pydeps` (Python). Else derive from import statements.

## Phase 2 (CDK): Read synthesized templates, Tier 2 (offline, preferred)

```bash
for t in cdk.out/*.template.json; do
  jq '[.Resources[].Type] | group_by(.) | map({type:.[0], n:length})' "$t"   # resource type inventory
  jq '.Resources | to_entries[] | {logicalId:.key, type:.value.Type, deps:(.value.DependsOn // []), props:(.value.Properties|keys)}' "$t"
done
```

CloudFormation resource fields to extract: the map KEY is the logical ID (strongest CDK provenance), `Type` (`AWS::Lambda::Function` -> AWS service), `Properties` (real sizes/ARNs/env incl. model IDs), `DependsOn` plus `Ref`/`Fn::GetAtt` in properties (edges), CDK path from `Metadata."aws:cdk:path"` (maps a logical ID back to `file:line` construct). Prefer the synthesized logical ID + CDK path over a bare construct grep when both exist.

## Phase 3: Live drift (AWS creds, optional, a person's only)

Pulumi: `pulumi preview --json` computes diff vs live cloud. CDK: `cdk diff` compares synth vs the deployed stack; `aws cloudformation get-template --stack-name <name>` reads the deployed template (Tier 1). All read-only. Never by an agent: the platform's agents have no AWS credentials. A person runs them when they want
drift detection.

## Resource type -> AWS service -> C4 element

Pulumi naming: `aws:<module>/<resource>:<Class>` (classic), `aws-native:<service>:<Resource>` (Cloud Control), `awsx:<service>:<Component>` (Crosswalk, expands to many resources), `eks:index:Cluster`. CDK synthesizes to CloudFormation types: `AWS::<Service>::<Resource>`. Both map to the same AWS service and C4 role; match on the AWS service column.

| Pulumi type | CloudFormation type (CDK synth) | AWS service | C4 role | Level |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `aws:s3/bucket:Bucket` | `AWS::S3::Bucket` | S3 | Data store | L200/L400 |
| `aws:lambda/function:Function` | `AWS::Lambda::Function` | Lambda | Serverless fn | L200/L300 |
| `aws:apigateway/restApi:RestApi`, `aws:apigatewayv2/api:Api` | `AWS::ApiGateway::RestApi`, `AWS::ApiGatewayV2::Api` | API Gateway | API container | L200 |
| `aws:sfn/stateMachine:StateMachine` | `AWS::StepFunctions::StateMachine` | Step Functions | Orchestrator | L200/L300 |
| `aws:sqs/queue:Queue`, `aws:sns/topic:Topic` | `AWS::SQS::Queue`, `AWS::SNS::Topic` | SQS / SNS | Messaging | L300 |
| `aws:events/rule:Rule` | `AWS::Events::Rule` | EventBridge | Event router | L300 |
| `aws:ec2/vpc:Vpc`, `awsx:ec2:Vpc` | `AWS::EC2::VPC` (+`Subnet`/`InternetGateway`/`NatGateway`) | VPC | Network boundary | L400 |
| `aws:dynamodb/table:Table` | `AWS::DynamoDB::Table` | DynamoDB | NoSQL store | L200/L400 |
| `aws:rds/cluster:Cluster`, `aws:rds/instance:Instance` | `AWS::RDS::DBCluster`, `AWS::RDS::DBInstance` | Aurora / RDS | Relational store | L200/L400 |
| `aws:opensearchserverless/collection:Collection` | `AWS::OpenSearchServerless::Collection` | AOSS (VECTORSEARCH) | Vector store | L200/L300 |
| `aws:ecs/service:Service`, `awsx:ecs:FargateService` | `AWS::ECS::Service` (+`TaskDefinition`) | ECS / Fargate | Container service | L200 |
| `eks:index:Cluster` | `AWS::EKS::Cluster` | EKS | K8s cluster | L200 |
| `aws:ecr/repository:Repository` | `AWS::ECR::Repository` | ECR | Container registry | L400 |
| `aws:iam/role:Role`, `aws:iam/policy:Policy` | `AWS::IAM::Role`, `AWS::IAM::Policy` | IAM | Identity / permission | L400 |
| `aws:kms/key:Key`, `aws:secretsmanager/secret:Secret` | `AWS::KMS::Key`, `AWS::SecretsManager::Secret` | KMS / Secrets Manager | Crosscutting (§8) | L400 |
| `aws:cloudwatch/logGroup:LogGroup`, `metricAlarm:MetricAlarm` | `AWS::Logs::LogGroup`, `AWS::CloudWatch::Alarm` | CloudWatch | Observability | L400 |
| `aws:cognito/userPool:UserPool` | `AWS::Cognito::UserPool` | Cognito | Auth | L200 |
| `aws:cloudfront/distribution:Distribution` | `AWS::CloudFront::Distribution` | CloudFront | CDN | L200 |
| `aws:codebuild/project:Project`, `aws:codepipeline/pipeline:Pipeline` | `AWS::CodeBuild::Project`, `AWS::CodePipeline::Pipeline` | CodeBuild / CodePipeline | CI/CD | L300 (deployment) |

CDK note: L2/L3 constructs synthesize to several CloudFormation resources (e.g., `lambda.Function` adds an `AWS::IAM::Role` and `AWS::Logs::LogGroup`). Group child resources under their construct path (`aws:cdk:path`) so the model mirrors author intent, not raw template noise.

### AI-on-AWS components (recognize and document)

| Pulumi type | CloudFormation type (CDK synth) | AWS service | C4 role |
|---|---|---|---|
| `aws:bedrock/agentKnowledgeBase:AgentKnowledgeBase` | `AWS::Bedrock::KnowledgeBase` | Bedrock Knowledge Base | RAG KB |
| `aws:bedrock/agentDataSource:AgentDataSource` | `AWS::Bedrock::DataSource` | Bedrock KB data source | S3 ingest |
| `aws:bedrock/agentAgent:AgentAgent` (+`AgentAlias`, `AgentActionGroup`) | `AWS::Bedrock::Agent`, `AWS::Bedrock::AgentAlias` | Bedrock Agents | Autonomous agent + tools |
| `aws:bedrock/guardrail:Guardrail` (+`GuardrailVersion`) | `AWS::Bedrock::Guardrail` | Bedrock Guardrails | AI safety filter |
| `aws:bedrock/agentcoreAgentRuntime:*` (+`Endpoint`) | `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::Runtime` (+`RuntimeEndpoint`) | Bedrock AgentCore | Production agent runtime |
| `aws:bedrock/agentcoreMemory:*` | `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::Memory` | AgentCore Memory | Session memory |
| `aws:bedrock/agentcoreGateway:*` (+`GatewayTarget`) | `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::Gateway` (+`GatewayTarget`) | AgentCore Gateway | Tool/API gateway w/ auth |
| (resource-based policy, SDK or CDK `CfnResourcePolicy`) | `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::ResourcePolicy` | AgentCore Runtime/Gateway cross-account policy | Crosscutting (§8), IAM model |
| `aws:bedrock/agentcoreBrowser:*`, `agentcoreCodeInterpreter:*` | `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::*` | AgentCore tools | Browser / code sandbox |
| `aws:bedrock/provisionedModelThroughput:*`, `customModel:*`, `inferenceProfile:*` | `AWS::Bedrock::ApplicationInferenceProfile` (PTU + custom-model fine-tune are API-only, no public CFN type) | Bedrock | PTU / fine-tune / cross-region inference |
| `aws:sagemaker/endpoint:Endpoint` (+`EndpointConfiguration`) | `AWS::SageMaker::Endpoint` (+`EndpointConfig`) | SageMaker | Real-time inference |
| `aws:sagemaker/model:Model`, `trainingJob:TrainingJob` | `AWS::SageMaker::Model` | SageMaker | Model artifact / training |
| `aws:sagemaker/pipeline:Pipeline` | `AWS::SageMaker::Pipeline` | SageMaker Pipelines | ML workflow |
| `aws:sagemaker/featureGroup:FeatureGroup` | `AWS::SageMaker::FeatureGroup` | SageMaker Feature Store | Feature serving |
| `aws:sagemaker/modelPackageGroup:ModelPackageGroup` | `AWS::SageMaker::ModelPackageGroup` | SageMaker Model Registry | Model versions |
| `aws:sagemaker/domain:Domain` | `AWS::SageMaker::Domain` | SageMaker Studio | ML platform |

**Bedrock Runtime and SageMaker training jobs are often SDK-only** (no IaC resource). Signal: Lambda/ECS env var `MODEL_ID`/`BEDROCK_MODEL_ID` + IAM `bedrock:InvokeModel`; or a `sagemaker:CreateTrainingJob` permission. In CDK these appear as `grantInvoke`/`addToRolePolicy` calls in source, not as a synthesized resource. Record as a flow edge, not a resource.

**Typical flows to capture as `flows` in the model:**
- Inference: User -> CloudFront? -> API Gateway -> Lambda/ECS -> Bedrock InvokeModel/InvokeAgent / SageMaker endpoint -> (KB retrieval via AOSS) -> response -> CloudWatch.
- Training: S3 data lake -> EventBridge -> Step Functions / SageMaker Pipeline -> Training Job -> S3 artifact -> Model Registry -> Endpoint -> CloudWatch drift -> retrain.
- RAG ingest: S3 docs -> Bedrock KB data source sync -> embedding model -> AOSS VECTORSEARCH.

## Security / cost / reliability signals (`_model/signals.json`)

Flag with severity + provenance. MUST aligns with the repository's own AWS rules (its SECURITY.md or INFRA.md, when it has one).

Property names below show the Pulumi form; the CloudFormation/CDK form is equivalent (e.g., `AuthType: NONE` on `AWS::Lambda::Url`, `BlockPublicAcls`/`PublicAccessBlockConfiguration` on `AWS::S3::Bucket`, `HttpTokens: optional` on the launch template). Match on intent, not exact key.

**Security (MUST):** Lambda Function URL `authorizationType`/`AuthType` `"NONE"`; IAM `Action`/`Resource` `"*"`; S3 missing `blockPublicAccess`/`PublicAccessBlockConfiguration`; Lambda permission `principal`/`Principal` `"*"`; Cognito `allowedOauthFlows` includes `"implicit"`; CORS `allow_origins ["*"]`; secrets in Lambda `environment.variables`/`Environment.Variables` (names like `PASSWORD`/`SECRET`/`KEY`); IMDSv1 (`httpTokens`/`HttpTokens` `"optional"`); SG `0.0.0.0/0` on 22/3389. **SHOULD:** missing encryption at rest; sensitive resource outside VPC; AOSS without KMS CMK.

**Cost (SHOULD):** SageMaker endpoint always-on without auto-scaling; Bedrock provisioned throughput vs utilization; Lambda `memorySize` > 3008 on light workloads; S3 without lifecycle rules; training on on-demand only (no Spot/savings plan).

**Reliability (SHOULD):** Lambda async without `deadLetterConfig`; Step Functions without `Retry`/`Catch`; SQS without `redrivePolicy`; SageMaker endpoint single `instanceCount: 1`; no CloudWatch alarms; Bedrock Agent without `guardrailConfiguration`.

## Model JSON schema (`_model/model.json`)

```json
{
  "meta": { "iac_tool": "pulumi|cdk", "tier": "1|2|3", "generated": "ISO8601", "projects": [], "stacks": [], "caveats": [] },
  "elements": [
    {
      "id": "stable-slug",
      "name": "inference-handler",
      "kind": "container|component|datastore|external|actor|ai",
      "iac_type": "aws:lambda/function:Function",
      "aws_service": "Lambda",
      "level": "L200",
      "project": "myproject",
      "stack": "prod",
      "provenance": { "urn": "urn:pulumi:prod::...", "logical_id": "InferenceFnXXXX", "cdk_path": "App/ProdStack/InferenceFn", "file": "src/api.ts", "line": 42 },
      "attrs": { "runtime": "python3.12", "model_id": "anthropic.claude-..." }
    }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "id-a", "to": "id-b", "kind": "invokes|reads|writes|depends|references", "label": "InvokeModel", "provenance": {} }
  ],
  "flows": [
    { "id": "inference", "level": "L300", "steps": [ {"from":"user","to":"apigw","label":"POST /invoke"} ] }
  ],
  "signals": [
    { "id": "sig-1", "category": "security|cost|reliability", "severity": "MUST|SHOULD|NIT", "title": "", "provenance": {} }
  ],
  "adr_candidates": [
    { "title": "Pulumi over CDK", "evidence_ids": [], "provenance": {} }
  ],
  "unverified": [ "note about anything inferred but not located" ]
}
```

**Provenance rule**: every element, edge, flow step, and signal carries `provenance` with the strongest anchor available: a Pulumi `urn`, a CloudFormation `logical_id` (+ `cdk_path`), or a `file:line`. Entries without provenance go in `unverified[]` and are excluded from generated diagrams.

# Level Model: L100 -> L400 mapped to C4 + arc42

The doc set ramps from overview to expert depth using the AWS session-level convention (100/200/300/400). Each level maps to a C4 abstraction and arc42 sections, so a new reader climbs from "what is this" to "exact resources" without re-reading.

## The four levels

| Level | Depth | Reader question | C4 | arc42 | Time to read |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **L100** | Overview | "What is this and who uses it?" | System Context | §1 Goals, §3 Context | 10 min |
| **L200** | Intermediate | "How is it structured?" | Container | §4 Strategy, §5 Building Block L1 | 20 min |
| **L300** | Deep | "How does it work inside and at runtime?" | Component + Dynamic | §5 Building Block L2, §6 Runtime | 30 min |
| **L400** | Expert | "What exactly runs, where, with what config?" | Deployment + resource detail | §7 Deployment, §8 Crosscutting | 45 min |

## What belongs at each level

### L100: Overview (System Context)
- The one system as a single box; the people/roles who use it; external systems it talks to (identity provider, third-party APIs, Bedrock as managed service if treated as external).
- No internal structure. No AWS service inventory. No protocols.
- Diagram: `C4Context`. Cap ~6-8 elements.
- Audience: everyone, including non-technical stakeholders.

### L200: Intermediate (Container)
- IaC stacks/apps as containers; major AWS services as named boxes (API Gateway, Lambda, SageMaker endpoint, S3, DynamoDB, vector store); cross-stack wiring via Pulumi StackReferences or CDK stack-to-stack refs / `Fn::ImportValue`.
- Each box: name + technology + one-line responsibility.
- Exclude deployment detail (replicas, load balancers, subnets); those are L400.
- Diagrams: `C4Container` for the architecture; `mindmap` for the stack/module map.
- Audience: architects, leads, new engineers building a mental model.

### L300: Deep (Component + Dynamic)
- Inside each non-trivial container: modules, Pulumi `ComponentResource` or CDK `Construct`/`Stack` classes, handlers, their responsibilities and interfaces.
- Runtime flows: the request/inference path and the training/data-pipeline path.
- Diagrams: `C4Component` per significant container; `sequenceDiagram` for request/inference flow; `flowchart LR` with subgraphs for ML training pipeline; `stateDiagram-v2` for job/model lifecycle.
- Audience: developers working in a specific area.

### L400: Expert (Deployment + resource detail)
- Real deployed resources with config (instance types, memory, runtimes), per environment (dev/staging/prod), VPC/subnet topology, CI/CD runtime.
- Crosscutting: IAM role model, tagging, secrets, encryption, model versioning/governance, observability.
- Data model at field level.
- Diagrams: `C4Deployment` (one per significant environment); `flowchart TB` with nested subgraphs for VPC/subnet/account; `erDiagram` for data model; `classDiagram` for the IaC component/construct hierarchy if it aids understanding.
- Audience: ops, infra engineers, security reviewers.

## Progressive disclosure rule

A fact appears at exactly one level (its home), and deeper levels add detail rather than restating. Example: S3 exists as a box at L200, its bucket policy and encryption at L400. The L200 prose links down to L400 rather than copying. This is the same single-source-of-truth rule enforced in `doc-plan.md`.

## Reading path for a new engineer

1. L100 `00-overview.md`: context (10 min)
2. L200 `01-containers.md` + `04-solution-strategy.md`: structure and why (35 min)
3. L300 `02-components.md` + `09-dynamic/`: internals and runtime (30 min, as needed per area)
4. L400 `03-deployment.md` + `05-crosscutting.md`: exact infra (45 min, for ops/security)

The plan should record, per generated doc, which level it sits at and which model element ids feed its diagrams.

| `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::Runtime` and `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::RuntimeEndpoint` are real CloudFormation resource types (added September 2025) | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/TemplateReference/AWS_BedrockAgentCore.md | 2026-10-28 |

The resource-type -> AWS-service -> C4-role mapping table in `extraction.md` is a living
reference. Bedrock AgentCore and Bedrock Agents ship new CloudFormation resource types
often; re-check `AWS::BedrockAgentCore::*` and `AWS::Bedrock::*` against the CloudFormation
Template Reference before relying on a type that is not in this table.

Decide the smallest correct way to build what your task asks.

Ladder concept adapted from [DietrichGebert/ponytail](https://github.com/DietrichGebert/ponytail)
and [addyosmani/agent-skills](https://github.com/addyosmani/agent-skills) (both MIT).

The `anti-slop` skill finds hand-rolled code and dead abstraction after it exists. This skill runs before, so the
code is never written. Cheaper by an order of magnitude.

## Step 0: Load Project Standards

If the repository has a STANDARDS.md (or INFRA.md), read it with `read_file`: its package managers, dependency
policy and size limits, and INFRA.md's approved services and SDKs. Else the defaults below. Cite those files rather
than restating them.

## Step 1: Understand Before Climbing

The ladder shortens the solution. It never shortens the reading.

- [ ] Read the code the change touches, end to end, including callers
- [ ] Find the existing pattern for this concern in this repo
- [ ] Confirm the requirement, not your reconstruction of it

A minimal change in the wrong place is a second bug, not a small diff.

## Step 2: The Ladder

Stop at the first rung that holds. Record which rung you stopped on.

| # | Rung | Test |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Does it need to exist? | Is this speculative, or required by the current request? |
| 2 | Already in this repo? | Search for the helper, type, or pattern before writing one (`run` `grep -rn <name> <dir>`, or `list_files` and `read_file`) |
| 3 | Standard library? | `itertools`, `dataclasses`, `pathlib`, `functools`, `Intl`, `URL`, `crypto` |
| 4 | Platform or framework native? | DB constraint over app check, CSS over JS, framework middleware over custom |
| 5 | Already-installed dependency? | Read the lockfile before adding anything |
| 6 | Official vendor SDK? | boto3, aws-cdk-lib L2, Powertools, Stripe SDK, Linear SDK |
| 7 | Minimum custom code | Only now. Smallest thing that satisfies the request |

Two rungs both work? Take the higher number only when it is more correct on edge cases,
not because it is more interesting.

## Step 3: Never Hand-Roll These

Custom implementations here are MUST findings. Use the named alternative.

| Concern | Use |
|---|---|
| Crypto, hashing, signing, JWT verify | Platform crypto library, vendor SDK verifier |
| Auth flows, token refresh, session rotation | Identity provider SDK (Cognito, Auth0, OIDC client) |
| Retry, backoff, jitter, circuit breaking | SDK built-in retry config, `tenacity`, Powertools |
| Date, time, timezone, duration arithmetic | `datetime` + `zoneinfo`; `date-fns` or `Intl.DateTimeFormat` in Node (TC39 `Temporal` ships behind `--harmony-temporal` as of Node 25, not yet stable; check `typeof Temporal` before relying on it unflagged) |
| CSV, YAML, TOML, INI, XML parsing | `csv`, `defusedcsv` for output, `PyYAML.safe_load`, `tomllib` |
| Schema validation and coercion | Pydantic, Zod. Never a hand-written `is_valid()` |
| Pagination, waiters, presigned URLs | SDK paginators, waiters, presigner |
| Connection pooling, rate limiting | Driver pool config, API Gateway throttling, SDK client reuse |
| ID generation | `uuid`, `secrets`, `ulid`, database identity column |
| Structured logging and tracing | `structlog`, Powertools Logger, OpenTelemetry SDK |
| Concurrency primitives | `asyncio`, `concurrent.futures`, framework task queue |
| Diffing, templating, path handling | `difflib`, Jinja2, `pathlib`, `path` |

For AWS specifically: prefer a managed service over code that emulates it. Infrastructure as code has its own
ladder, so use it rather than improvising: the `cdk-engineer` skill for CDK, the `terraform-engineer` skill for
Terraform. See also the `aws-serverless` skill.

## Step 4: Verify the API Before Calling It

Rung 6 fails badly when the method does not exist. Before first use of any SDK surface:

- [ ] Import resolves in this environment
- [ ] Method name and signature confirmed against the installed source (`node_modules/`, the virtual environment's
      `site-packages/`, the type stubs), since the sandbox has no network to fetch docs
- [ ] Return shape confirmed, not assumed
- [ ] Version in the lockfile matches the docs you read

Full protocol: the `code-review` skill's api-verification reference. Guessing a plausible method name is the most
common failure at this rung.

## Step 5: Dependency Admission

Adding a package is a supply-chain decision, so admit it only when every one of these holds:

- [ ] Nothing at rungs 1 to 5 covers it
- [ ] Saves more than roughly 50 lines of code you would otherwise own
- [ ] Actively maintained, release within the last 12 months
- [ ] Licence compatible with this project (check copyleft against distribution plans)
- [ ] Name checked against typosquat variants of the package you intended
- [ ] Pinned to an exact version, the lockfile updated in your change
- [ ] Transitive footprint reviewed for a small utility

Decide a new dependency before your first command: `install_dependencies` is the one command with the package
registries, and it runs once, before any other. A dependency you find you need later is a reason to `finish` and say
so, not to work around the sandbox.

Reject a dependency that wraps something the stdlib already does. See the `security-audit` skill for CVE and
supply-chain checks on the resulting tree.

## Step 6: Refuse These Abstractions

Do not create, unless the second consumer exists today:

| Pattern | Rule |
|---|---|
| Interface, Protocol, or ABC | Needs two implementations, or one real test double at a layer boundary |
| Factory | Needs more than one product |
| Config option | Needs a caller that sets a non-default value |
| Feature flag | Needs a plan to toggle it |
| Wrapper or adapter | Needs to add behaviour, not only forward arguments |
| Base class | Composition first. Inheritance only for a genuine substitutable type |
| New package or module | Fewest files that hold the change. Extract on the third use, not the first |

A single-implementation port is legitimate when it enforces the dependency rule and has a fake in tests. Detail:
the `python-engineer` skill's architecture-patterns reference.

## Step 7: Performance Decisions Made at Write Time

Cheap to get right now, expensive to retrofit. Not premature optimisation.

- [ ] No query inside a loop. Batch, join, or `IN` clause instead
- [ ] Bulk SDK call over per-item calls (`batch_write_item`, `send_message_batch`)
- [ ] Right container: set or dict for membership, not list scan
- [ ] Stream large payloads. No `read()` of an unbounded file or response
- [ ] No blocking I/O inside an async path
- [ ] Client, connection, and session objects created once, reused
- [ ] Pagination bounded. No unbounded `scan` or `SELECT *`
- [ ] Known quadratic loops flagged with the input size that breaks them

Measure before optimising anything beyond this list. Profiling: the `perf-debug` skill.

## Step 8: Import and Scaffolding Hygiene

- [ ] Absolute imports only. No relative parent traversal (ruff `TID252`)
- [ ] All imports at module top, except a documented cycle or cost break (ruff `E402`)
- [ ] Same package imported one way per file, not top-level and deferred
- [ ] No unused imports or re-exports with no consumer (`F401`, knip, vulture)
- [ ] No barrel file that re-exports a whole package for one symbol
- [ ] No empty placeholder file, directory, or `TODO` stub submitted

## Step 9: When Not to Be Minimal

Never remove or defer, whatever the diff size:

- Validation at trust boundaries
- Error handling that prevents data loss or silent corruption
- Authentication, authorisation, encryption, secret handling
- Accessibility basics
- Anything the task explicitly requested

A deliberate shortcut with a known ceiling gets a comment naming the ceiling and the
upgrade path: `# ceiling: single-process lock, move to Redis if multi-instance`.

## Step 10: Report

Put this in your `finish` summary:

```
## Build decision: [what was requested]

| Rung reached | Choice | Rejected |
|---|---|---|
| 3 (stdlib) | `functools.lru_cache` | custom TTL cache class (~80 lines to own) |

- Skipped: [abstraction or option], add when [trigger]
- Dependencies added: none / [name==version, why rungs 1-5 failed]
- API verified: [symbol, source read]
- Perf decisions: [batching, pooling, streaming choices]
- Ceilings accepted: [comment locations]
```

## Self-Check

- [ ] Read the touched code before choosing a rung
- [ ] Grepped this repo before writing a new helper
- [ ] Nothing on the never-hand-roll list was hand-rolled
- [ ] Every new SDK call verified against real source or docs
- [ ] New dependencies passed all admission checks
- [ ] No abstraction created for a consumer that does not exist
- [ ] Step 7 performance list checked
- [ ] Step 9 items intact

Gate the completion claim you are about to make.

Adapted from the verification discipline in [obra/superpowers](https://github.com/obra/superpowers) (MIT).

Most skills in this library audit code. This one audits your own statements about that code. Apply it whenever a
claim about state is about to go into a submission, a review, a gate record or a finish.

## The Rule

No completion claim without verification evidence produced in the current turn.

Evidence from an earlier turn is stale. Code changed since then. Re-run the command (with `run`).

## Step 1: Name the Proving Command

State the claim, then the single command whose output would falsify it.

| Claim | Proving command | Not proof |
|---|---|---|
| Tests pass | `pytest -q` / `pnpm vitest run` exit 0, failure count 0 | An earlier run, "should pass" |
| Build succeeds | `pnpm build` / `uv build` / `cdk synth` exit 0 | Linter passing, type checker passing |
| Infrastructure code is valid | `cdk synth` / `terraform validate` exit 0 (offline; never a deploy) | The code looking right |
| Types check | `pyright` / `tsc --noEmit` exit 0 | Editor showing no red squiggles |
| Lint clean | `ruff check` / `biome check` exit 0 | Partial run on one file |
| Bug fixed | Test reproducing the original symptom now passes | Code changed, cause understood |
| Regression test works | Red-green cycle verified (Step 4) | Test passes once |
| Requirements met | Line-by-line checklist against the request | Tests passing |
| Another agent's task done | Its patch read (`read_patch`), its gate record or findings read (`read_gate_record`, `read_findings`) | Its finish summary, the task's title |
| Performance improved | Before and after measurement, same conditions | Reasoning about complexity |

If no command can falsify the claim, the claim is an opinion. Label it as one.

## Step 2: Run It Fresh and Complete

- Run the full command, not a subset. One passing test file does not prove the suite.
- Read the exit code `run` answers first, then the output. `run` takes argv, not a shell line, so there is no pipe
  to hide it; a wrapper script that swallows the exit code hides it just the same.
- Read the whole output. Count failures. Check for skipped, xfailed, or deselected tests.
- A suite that collected 0 tests exits 0. That is not a pass.
- Watch for a stale result from a cache or watch mode: clear `.pytest_cache`, stop `vitest
  --watch`, and re-run with `--no-cache` / a one-shot flag if the runner supports it.

For example `run` with `["python", "-m", "pytest", "-q"]`: exit code first, then the counts.

## Step 3: Compare Output to Claim

| Result | Action |
|---|---|
| Output confirms the claim | State the claim with the evidence inline |
| Output contradicts the claim | State actual status, then fix (a fixer or builder) or record it (a reviewer, a gate). Never soften the wording instead |
| Command failed to run | Report the gap as a gap. Missing tooling is not a pass |
| Output ambiguous | Say so, name what would resolve it |

Report format (your finish summary):

```
Tests: 47 passed, 0 failed (uv run pytest -q, exit 0)
Types: pyright 0 errors
Lint:  ruff clean
Not verified: integration suite (needs AWS credentials)
```

## Step 4: Regression Tests Need a Red Phase

A test that has never failed proves nothing. It may assert on the wrong thing.

1. Write the test.
2. Run it. It passes with the fix in place.
3. Undo the fix only: write the changed lines back as they were with `write_file` (never `git stash` or
   `git revert`: the checkout's git is the harness's).
4. Run again. It has to fail: if it passes, the test does not cover the bug.
5. Write the fix back. Run again. It passes.

Only after step 4 fails may you call the test a regression test. Full protocol: the `tdd` skill.

## Step 5: Verify Another Agent's Work Independently

Another agent's finish, or a task's title, is a claim, not evidence. When your task judges another agent's work (a
review, a gate, a final go):

- [ ] Read the patch (`read_patch`, every page), not the summary
- [ ] The files it claims to change are the files it changes
- [ ] Re-run the proving command yourself when your role runs code; read the gate record (`read_gate_record`) when it
      does not
- [ ] Check for files changed outside the task's scope

## Step 6: Requirements Checklist

Tests passing proves the code runs. It does not prove you built what was asked.

Re-read your task (and the run's issue, when it has one). List each requirement. Mark each: met (with evidence),
partial (with what is missing), or not started. Report gaps before claiming completion.
Scope creep counts as a gap: name anything built that was not requested.

## Rationalisations to Refuse

| Excuse | Reality |
|---|---|
| "Should work now" | Run it |
| "I am confident" | Confidence is not evidence |
| "Linter passed" | Linters do not compile or execute |
| "Types check" | Type checkers do not run tests |
| "The other agent said success" | Read the patch or the record |
| "Same as last run" | Code changed since then |
| "Only a comment changed" | Run it, the command is cheap |
| "Partial check is enough" | Partial output proves the part you ran |
| "Different wording avoids the rule" | The rule covers meaning, not phrasing |

## Red Flags in Your Own Draft

Stop and run the command if your draft contains:

- Hedges: "should", "probably", "seems to", "appears to", "ought to"
- Satisfaction before evidence: "Done", "Fixed", "All set", "Working now"
- Any past-tense success verb with no command output above it
- A `submit_work`, `write_review`, `write_gate_record` or `finish` about to happen with no proving command in this
  turn

## Step 7: Verdict

| Verdict | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **VERIFIED** | Every claim has fresh command output in this turn |
| **PARTIAL** | Some claims verified. Unverified ones named explicitly |
| **UNVERIFIED** | No proving command run. Do not claim completion |
| **BLOCKED** | Proving command cannot run here. Name the missing prerequisite |

Report `PARTIAL` honestly rather than upgrading it to `VERIFIED`. An honest gap costs one follow-up task. A false
pass costs a production incident.

## Self-Check

- [ ] Named a falsifiable command for every claim in the response
- [ ] Ran each command in this turn, not an earlier one
- [ ] Read exit codes, not only stdout
- [ ] Regression tests went through a red phase
- [ ] Another agent's work checked against its patch or record
- [ ] Requirements checked line by line against the task
- [ ] Unverifiable items labelled, not omitted
